articles.title: PROGRESS.
articles.text:
PROGRESS.

How many of us there are who hear and
use the word "progress," and yet have but
little notion of its meaning, of the immensity
and. complexity of the truths which it implies.
Ip sooth, the conception of progress is not
simple or easy, but, on the contrary, highly
complicated, and the very ideas of which it is
composed have only been formed by man with
great difficulty after the lapse of a long time.
I do not refer to any partial improvement like
the accumulation of wealth, the increase of
material comfort, or the advance ,of seientifie
knowledge, nor to that which has been aocom-
plished at any particular period or by any
one people. Each partial progress has its
place, and its relative importance, and has
contributed its share towards the general
'result. The progress which I shall try to
explain, is that of the whole human race, in
the past, in the present, and in the future—in
other words, the progress of Humanity. When
we understand. the nature of the whole, then,
and then only, can we estimate the value of
its parts. I shall devote several articles to
this subject, because, according to my opinion,
it is the most important of all subjects; at
once the foundation of all systematic know-
ledge, and the source whence we must derive
our power over social events. Moreover, the
conception of the progress of Humanity leads
directly to the true objeot of human endeavour,.
the reorganisation of social life upon a higher
model with a nobler end. The history of pro-
gress is the history of man, the record of man's
experience; which, when rightly understood,
explains the past, enables us to comprehend
the present, and gives us insight into the ten-
dency and
,course of future events. We judge
a man's character by what we know of him.
When we are familiar with the mode in which

he has conducted himself, we can tell with
tolerable accuracy how he will behave under a
given set of circumstances. And the more
intimate we are with the facts of his life; tho
more certain we are as to what he will do.
This is only one example of the way in which
human acts depend upon experience. Each
of us measures his powers by what he has
done, liVe soldom take a leap into absolute
darknese:-- •

"There is a-history in all moult
Figuring the nature of the times deceased;
The which observed, a man may prophecy,
'With a near aim, of the main chance of
,things
As yet not come to life • which mu their seeds
And weak beginnings, fie intreasured.
Such things become the hatch- ana brood of
This,- *hick is,trde of the, individual life, is
of the race. "The present is the product
of the past,- and is big with the future."
History, then, is not narrative or annals, nut
the descriptions of sieges and battles, of
intrigues of kings and courtiers and such like
things, but the real sequence of events con-
stituting progress. This sequence is not the
result Of chance. Beneath the great variety of
facts, and midst the complexity of endless
detail, there has .always, been a definite,
Orderly Movement, thOugh men at first could
not perceive it; there his been a real chain of
successive events linked together by proper
soiontifio connection, each event being, depen‘:-
dent on those that preceded it. -

it must be obvious to any thoughtful per-
son, that before Men could have become
conscions that progress was taking place, a
certain amount of progress must have been
accomplished. Until a certain stage had been
reached, it Would have been imperceptible.
When we look at a distant object, as for
example, a ship at sea, at first we cannot
make- out whether it is moving or not. After
a time, we observe that- it has moved, and
from that result we infer that it is moving.
We need not; therefore', be surprised to find
that in ancient tizzies 111011 did not even dream
of progress taking place. The idea has' been
slowly evelved. " The first germ of it was due
to Christianity. For that religion taught that
•
man might by effort attain to a higher and
better state of existence. it was the germ of
the• grand moralising idea of progress, now
beginning to bear fruit. But in that barren
form—the conoeption being really limited to
the superior excellence of the Christian rules
to the law or-Moies—it was of little social
value—a progress of only one step; a con-
ception ignoring the results of the Greek and
Roman eivilizations, which had preceded and
paved the way for Christianity. The noble
work- which Christianity had to do was to
matinee Western. Europe. Before that was
accomplished, how could there be an adequate
idea of human progress? Besides, some of
the Christian doctrines are opposed and oon-
tradictory to the conception of progress. Such
as the deadly, paralysing belief, that man on
this earth of ours is but a stranger and a
sojourner in a foreign, land—a dogma hostile
to progress, in so far as it tends to withdraw
man's attention and efforts from the true
sphere of his Work avvay from the world, and
from the duties owing to his fellow men. Or
the monstrous anti-social fiction still taught
by Christian teachers, upon which we can only
look with sorrow and pity, that labour is a
degradation which has been imposed upon
man, the result of a divine, curse, and the
punishment of human sin. Or that still more
revolting story, which paints to woman as the
origin of evil, as the cause and source of
man's misfortunes.

So far from men having in past times any
strong convictions about their own progress,
we find that they have generally despised and
reviled their immediate predecessors, or those
less civilized peoples with whom they were in
contact. The Greeks and Ronattris looked upon
other nations as barbarians. It is common
now to hear educated Englishmen depreciating
Eastern civilizations, which they have never
taken the trouble to study. Christians re-
garded the great Polytheistio systems as
abominations. ' Protestants have reviled Ca-
tholics, and, have denied that Catholicism was
the instrument of progress in the middle ages.
And bifore the advent of the first French revo-
lution, the common creed flung down by Rev's-
EA:I73 and adopted more or less by the Western

world, was that the whole modern movement
was nothing but a gigantic mistake—a depar-
ture from the state of nature. Instead, of
progress, men believed in degeneration. They
despised, instead of being grateful to, the age
from which they had sprung, and to which
they owed all that they possessed. They
lcailted back with extraordinary reverence to
some more remote ancestors, whom they fan-
cied to have enjoyed greater physical strength,
to have been more beautiful, and 'Are perfect
than themselves. And if we consider the nature
of the great political and social facts, with
which men in the early Christian days were
confronted, namely, the decay of the Greek civi-
lisation, and the more recent break-up of the Ito-
-man Enipireof the West, we can easily see that
it was impossible for the most powerful mind
at that time to discern the true explanation
of these stupendous facts; to see that partial
decay and retrogression, that failure and col-
lapse were, after all, only parts, and neces-
sary parts, or one univeisal movement of the
progress of Humanity. As I said before, a
sufficient progress had not been accomplished,
the historical data were not enough, history
was as yet impossible. Still, before the con-
clusion of the middle ages men began to per-
ceive, dimly it is true, but still to perceive that
mankind was moving on towards a higher
perfection. Catholicism was seen to be
• superior both to Polytheism, and to Judaism.
'Feudalism, with all its defects and weaknesses,
was recognized as a distinct advance upon the
Roman system. There was nothing, however,
in all this which came near the conviction,
which day by day is gaining ground, that pro-
gress is a fundamental principle, the end and
purpose of social life.
But while we accord full justice to the
grandeur of the work accomplished in the
middle ages by Feudal institutions and the
Catholic Church, we must remember that
Feudalism and Catholicism were quite incon-
sistent with modern civilization, and that the
ideas upon which they rested had necessarily
to be discredited' and washed away. This was
effected, to different degrees in the various
countries Of Western Europe, by a negative
and destructive movement which we call the
revolutionary phase of modern society. This
destruction, in some shape or other, was in-
evitable. • It was requisite to clear the way for
the modern era, and so far revolutionary ideas
and actions were progressive. That tithe is
past. None are so retrograde now as the re-
volutionists. Their creed is powerful only to
destroy, it cannot construct. They only pro-
long the state of anarchy and chaos in which
we are. They constitute the chief obstacle to
the true solution of our difficulties. The Con-
servative notion of reverting to the theological
and political ideas of the past as the cure for
the present evils is untenable. So is the
revolutionary idea of the future altogether
independent of the past. Both are alike un-
true and impossible. We cannot go back,
neither can we deny that past by which we
have been moulded, which is both the current
and source of our life.

The only issue from the present difficulties,
the only hope of the fu4tre, consists in this—
that the whole past of Humanity has been a
preparation for that which is to come—that
from the beginning of Western civilization,
underneath, and often in spite of the various
political and religious systems that have pre-
vailed, the elements and principles of a new
life have been silently and slowly, but irre-
sistibly growing. I shall endeavour to trete°
the outline of the rise and development of the
elements of the new order. The effete rem-
nants of the old order, based upon war, and
, believed to be subject to arbitrary inter-
,
I ference, have to give place to a far higher
state of existence, for which we are already
ripe, founded by means of positive knowledge,
by peaceful industrious activity, whose end is
progress.

HENRY CROMPTO.Y.

THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT
ACT.

As this Act will again be brought under
the consideration of the forthcoming Trades
Congress, it may be useful to briefly trace its
history and the causes which led to its

enactment. We all know that previous to
passing Mr. BiIUCE'S little one-clause Act in
1870, for the protection. of the funds of trades
unions these combinations were not considered
lawfuli: It was therefore admitted on all
sides that provision ought to be made to pro-
tect the funds of these unions, and although
Parliament could find time to pass 288 pri•
vale and public Acts in 1869, and 293 in
1870, chiefly in the interest of the wealthier
classes, it could only find time to pass a little
one-clause Act in the interest of the working
classes during these two sessions.
The Trades Union Bill, which had been pro-
mised in 1860, was shelved until 1871, to be
brought out again, cut and dried, to suit the
intereit of employers and capitalists. Now, it
ought to be borne in mind that when the
Trades Union Bill was first promised no such
thing as a Criminal Law Araeridment Act was
spoken of then. Instead, however, of the
promised Trades Union Bill, pure oral
simple, being brought in, the Bill was
out in two; the worst half being
made a penal enactment passed quickly
through the Commons, and the finishing
touch of stringency, given to it by the Lords,
without trades unionists being consulted about
it in any way.
In 1869, after a Trades Union Bill had
been promised, the Trades Congress which met
at Birmingham that year had a long and
animated discussion as to what the provisions
of that Bill should be, and the unanimous
opinion of that Congress was that the old
Combination Laws should berepealed, and that
trades unionists should stand in -the same
position before the law as all other societies or
associations of men, and that no legislaifon
whatever further than this was required.
It was a mystery for some time why and
how the decision of the Birmingham Trades
Congress was set aside and legislation ad-
mitted to be necessary. An explanation of the
way this was brought about, was, however,
given by Mr. GEORGE HOWELL, in his letter to
the BEE-HIVE of Jane 7th, which is, no doubt,
the correct one. Mr. HOWELL says in the last
paragraph of his letter—" One thing I must
add, in conclusion, that I have always opposed
all legislation on the subject, excepting the
repeal of the retuna.nt of the old Combination
Laws, but we were always advised by our
middle-class friends that Some further legisla-
tion was necessary, and I with others re-
luctantly consented." So that, it appears, we
were advised to accept legislation on the re-
commendation of certain middle-class friends.
And here was the mistake. There was no
necessity for legislation at all, other than the
repeal of tha old Combination Laws and legal-
ising these unions, and making their membera
amenable only to the common statute law
with respect to acts of violence, fraud, or
intimidation, the same as the members of all
other societies or associations.

Once having admitted that legislation was
necessary (other than legalising these unions),
no one could tell where it would begin or
where it would end. All legislation beyond
giving a legal status to trades unions was
certain to be of a penal character. Surely it
is the duty of trades unionists and their
friends to put their feet firmly down 'against
this kind of legislation. A penal enactment
for the special persecution of trades unionists,
however moderate it may appear, will always
be applied with severity against them, and,
however mild its provisions may seem, it is
a penal enactment after all, notwithstanding
all attempts to patch it up or mend it. How-
ever, there will, no doubt, have to be soul°
mending done to this Criminal Law Amend-
ment Act before we can secure its total repeal.
But such amendment onght to came from the
framers of the Act and their supporters, and
not from trades unionists. If they have seen
the injustice which has been perpetrated under
this Act, and have become ashamed of their
handy work, and show signs of repentance,
and desire to amend the Act so as to mitigate
its severity, by all moans let it be accepted,
and demand its total repeal all the same.
There is all the difference in the world be-
tween the promoters of this Act proposing its
amendment and a proposition of this kind
coming from trades unionists themselves. 111
the former ease the framers of the Act' admit

its injustice and show signs,o,f mentance. In
the latter cese, any propositidti of the kind
coming from trades unionists, would be con-
siderei a final settlement of the matter by
themselves, and they would thus become ac-
cissories to an Act which would still leave
them surrounded by the meshes of a penal
enactment specially and invidiously directed
against
_them. And thus, as Air. ALBERT
CuomPror very correctly and forcibly paints
out by the quotation in his admirable letter
ig the 8.-Etive on the 21st of Jane last—" It
was not mine enemy that hath done this
thing; then I could have borne it. But it
was thou, mine own familiar friend."

It is not, however, in consequence ' of its. ,
heiug. a special' onttetnient that objection is
taken to the Criminal Law Amendment Act.
It.. is in consequbace of its being a penal enaet-
ment specially and, unjustly directed, against
trades unionists, There- always must be a
speciality about all legislatien, which, how-
ever, may be made the very reverse of, nnjust
or oppressive. The truth of this in very well
put by Mr. VERNON HARCOURT in his letter in
the BEE-HIVE of June the 28th last. Mr.
VERNON HARCOURT very correctly states that—
"A great deal of our le,gislation is, and always
must be, special, in order to meet special evils
and special circumstances. The Factory Acts
which limited the hours of labour were special
Acts to reraedy special evils The Mines

special legislation. to deal with special eases."
Precisely so. But we must seloct special Ads'
the antithesis. of each other to contrast and
judge of the character of, their speciality.
There is the Criminal Law Amendment Act,
whieh is a whip of scorpions in the' hands of
employers and magistrates to scourge any
unwary trades unionist they may lay hold of. ,
Whereas, the special features of the 'Mines
Regulation Act are 'just and humane, and
hold out the olive branch of peace, and:gives
protection to the working
,nainers. So that it is
not the speciality of any Act so much as its
provisions which makes it either good, or bad.
Again, it is aUeged that the law is not strong
enough without this Aot to punish violence,
threats, or intimidation. Not strong ienough,
forsooth Do not the daily records of our
police courts show that the common ordinary
statute law reaches and punishes every case of
the kind that comes before-them ? Theref are
some people, from whom stre expect better'
things, who seer; to speak of trades unionists,
and those Who Oppose this Act and du,ire its
repeal as if we were desirous of prohibiting'
punishment for "overt acts of violence." Mr.
VERNON 4ARCOURT, in his letter which I have ,
referred to,, says—" If those who demand such
a.:repeal require that no prohibition against
overt acts of violence, . intimidation, and
racilestation .shall, be 'enacted, I have already
Baird I cannot concur in such a proposal."
But whoever made any such unreasonable'
, •
" Proposals ?" Certaioly not those who think
thi Act most harsh and unjust, not trades
unionists:either as far as Iltiow, and I have
had thousands of them under ma during the
last twenty-five years. . Mr. VERNON HAR-
COURS may not be aware that at the time the
outrage was committed by BROADHEAD, at
gbeffield, the London, . and otheF trades
Councils, sent deputations to Sheffield to in-
quire into the matter, and were among. the
first to desire the punishment of Ihtost)l449.
It is not that they are opposed to punishment
for 1‘ overt acts of violence, •Sze.” What
they really require is that they should be
placed before the common statute law the
same as the, members of any other soeiety,
Corporation, or body of men, both with regard
to the embezzlement of funds, violenee, inti-
midation, or any other ollenco against the law,
and that all other penal legislation should be
repealed..
No doubt the Bill prepared by Mr. VERNON
HARCOURT, With the sanction of the Parlia-
mentary Committee, will, if enacted, mitigate
the severify of the Act of 1.571 (whioh Mr.
Bax6E says gives the' power of indicting any
one on a Criminal charge who "may be stand-
ing opposite the gates of any factory or
workshop where a dispute is 'going on'),
and, therefore, trades unionists may accept it
and demand the repeal of all penal legislation
411 the same, including the Master end

Servants' Act, which is not much better, A
Bill of this kind ought to be prepared ty
trades unionists so as to place on record their
wishes and desires, and they cannot do this
better than by preptiring a Bill of their own.
It is to be hoped that a Bill of this kind will
be presented to, and have the sanction of, the
forthcoming Trades Congress, to pave the way
to its enactment by the nest Parliament, and
that a goodly number of trades unionists Will
find their .way to the House- of Commons to
support it.

ALFRED A. WALTON.

A great working men's meeting was held on
Tuesday evening in Exeter Hall, to eipresEi
sympAthy with, and afford suppoit to, the move-
ment now taking place for the purpose of im-
proving the position in the social seale of the
agricultural labourer. Upon the platform was
Mr. Thomas Hughes, M.P., Sir C. Dilke, Sir
Charles Treyslyan, Archbishop Manning, Mr.
Samuel Morley, M.P., Mr. W. Fowler, M.P.,
Mr. Campbell, L.P. (Rugby); Mr. Jay, J.P.
(Beamtr.ee) ; Mr. Cox, J.P. (Be}per) ; Rev. W.
Roberts, Rev. W. Attenborough, Mr. Frederick
Young, Mr. Lloyd Jones, Mr. Carvell Williams,
Mr. S. Whitstone, Mr: Henry Taylor, Mr.
G. Mitchell, Mr. Applegarth, Mr. Joseph Arch
(President Agricultural Labourer' Union), Mr.
Mundella, M.P., Mr. George Potter, Sir John
Bennett, Mr. Daniel Guile, and leading men from
trade societies. In ,spite of the unfavourable
state of the weather, there wee a large attendance,
and great enthusiasm was manifested during the
proceedings.

Mr. George Potter said he had to move that, in
the unavoidaVe absence of the Lord Mayor, Mr.
Samuel Morley be reversted to take the chair,
Alder Man Sir Sohn Bennett seconded the Motion,
which was agreed to unanimousbr.
The Chairman said he was anxious to express
in a very few words the sympathy as well as the
admiration which he felt towards these who had
been conducting the cause of the agricultural
labourer during the past few. Months. (ChOers.)
The small farmers, as a class, weto as much en-
titled to support as the agricultural labourers, and
therefore, he was there to show his sympathy, not
merely by words, but in a more substantial manner
--(cheers)---to help those men to help themselves,
he would desire to avoid everything which could
tend to widen, while his earnest wish would be to
heal, the breach which might have arisen in many
quarters. Ile bed watched the utterances which
had fallen from the agricultural labourers, and he
had the pleasure of some personal intercourse with
Mr. A.reh---(cheore)—and he thought there was
much cause for thankfulnees that awl a man had
been forced into the front rank, a 3nan so well
qualified to tell the sad tale of his class to the
public. (Cheers.) Ile had no hesitation in ex-
, pressing the opinion that the wagea of the Agri-
cultural labourer in many parts would be found to
be Bs. and Os. per week, and that if there were
what were called perquisites it was a most undo.
sirable and unhealthy condition of things. It was
clear that in some parts they gore -fifty-six weeks
of work in the year, for they hardly ever knew
when their work was done, toiling for fourteen and
fifteen hours a day. Men who had been struggling
for nine, and even eight houre, as a day's wyris,
would agree with him that that was a state of
things which needed a public expression of opinion
as much as the miserable wages they re4oived,
and the miserable houses which they occupied.
(Hear, hoar.) It was most desirable that the men
should be permitted to state their own case to the
meeting; and, trusting that no subject foreign to
its object would be introduced, he would call on
three representatives of the agricultural labourers
to speak for themselves. (Cheers.)
Mr. Ball, of Lincolnshire, then addressed the
meeting. He had worked as a boy for twopence
a day, breakfasting on bread and water, and
dining on bread and a beiring. He contended that
was not honest to toilers in the field. It was
possible, on the eurrent wage,' for a man with a
wife and a moderate family to live. He had been
e total abstainer for twenty-three years, and he
tried, by the strictest economy, to pay every one
their own, and had been charged with carelessness
because he had not been able to meet demands
when they were due. Working honestly he had
never been without necessities in his family
which were never met, wants never supplied, and
privations often endured. He had often been
ivithOut bread and without flour, though he had
not been so badly off as thousands. The pay was
now 15s. et week, though two years since it was
only 13s. Gd. The rise he attributed to the
agitation. (Hear, hear.) The pay was better
there than in vine parts of England, because
Lincolnshire was near the North, and men drifted
off until now there were not enough to cultivate
the soil properly. Men hired by the year had
perquisites, but, the farmer being the best scholar,
the labourer was often oversighted in the bargain.
The perquisite was a barrel of beer in harvest-
time. For years they had been trying in Lincoln-
shire to do away with the small holders of land,
who were now in an almost ruinous condition, so
that the only stepping.stone for the labourer was
removed. The system of yearly hired servants had
brought them under a systena of tyranny. Sinai'
holdings w ere thrown lett) large farms, the

ta-

rainier took the cottage, and said If You
live here you Work for tae; end at what wage
I like to give yolt." It was not fair that
beasts of burden fihould 'work eight 410'0
while men were worked sixteen; but, pro-
vided they could get sufficient food and raiment,
they would not complain of the work, but till they
got those necessities they woula not cease to
agitate. (Cheers.) Referring to the causes of the
agricultural labourers, he demanded education for
their children, sufficient food and clothing, habita-
tions fit for human beings, and admission to the
right of citizenship. (Cheers.)

'Mr. Mitchell, who repreeented Somereetshire,
said he had often suffered the pangs of hunger
behind the plough when a lad of nineteen, and he
had Worked from six in the morning to ten o'clock
without having two pennyworth of food within
him, though he had plenty of sour cider, which
was what they; called perquisites. Even with that
amount of labour the farmer was not satisfied.
The cider they got was the third :runnings—
(laughter)—the first being sent away to London,
the second sold in the neighbourhood, and the
third given to the labourers. He had early left
in disgust, and then the wages were 7s. a weak--
rose after to Be. Having heard of the high prices
in. the North, he had gone and prospered, and now
he desired to work for his hungry-belliea brethren
who remained. The living was tea-kettle broth
for breakfast. Two or three little pieces of bread
were put in the breakfast-pot, which hold three
quarts, and then the bread wits soaked with hot
water. For dinner they got a few'potatoes and a
square inch of bacon fried in the pan for a faintly
of seven, the fat going on the potatoes, and that
piece of bacon being the father's dinner. For tea
they soaked burned bread and put a little treacle
in it, that being carried to the husband in the field
by the woman. For supper they got little pieces
of bread and ekim milk cheese. For dwellings lee
them look in the Builder of the present week; but
he knew of thirteen huddling together in one
room, on what they called a shakedOwn, like
hounds in a kennel. (Shame.) Last week he hid
spoken to an old man at Yeovil, whose master told
him he could not give hini more than 6s. a week,
and who he said he was then literally starving:
He would do hi best te elevate the poor men of
that part of the country, and run all risks of the
horsepond. (Loud cheers.)

Mr. Arch, President' of the National Labourore
Union, then detailed his own eXPeriences us a
labourer. Ile had, he Said, for many years re-
fused to work for lea e than is. 6d. a day, which
waá Mice all that he received; but the reason why
i;.a was able to do so was because when he could
not get More at home, he went somewhere else:
Others, however, were not equally fortunate, but
he hoped that the union which Led been formed
would result in establishing a bettor state of things.
Only that morning ho had heard of a farmer in
Oxfordehire who rented a farm 4nder the Duke of
Marlborough, who went to two Cottages under
him with the police, and. turned out the wives and
children of the occupiers into the street, simply
beeause they had dared to assert their rights as
Englishmen, and had joined the Labourers' Union.
But while grievances such as were inflicted on
thorn continued to exist, they would nctver cease
to agitate against the injustice. (Cheers.) Ali
the labourer desired was to be treated like a man.
There was room enough in this country for all its
labourers; but if they. who made its wealth hy..the
sweat of their brows were not to be better housed
than the beasts of the field and to receive no
better food than bread and onions and potatoes,
with 21 lbs. of meat a week, for a family
consisting of four or five persons, its had been
is own case for weeks and Weeks, then he
would say that it was
.a 'disgrace to the country
that they should be kept here to stave, and that
it would be bettor they should be sent to live
more like human beings in 'America. But the
Subject was one which was now moviug the coun-
try from one eud to the other, and it behoved the
tenant farmers to look to it, for it would be a
serious affair for them when there cams to be two
masters to one man. If the landlords of this
country and the tenant farmers continued tO make
the union men suffer as they had done by turniug
them out into the btreot with no shelter, or means
of support, the result would be that the labourer
would quit a land whore he was used like a
more machine in the hands of the money-monger-
ing few. The labourer meant to be no longer
starved or trampled upon, and if he could not get
a fair share of the wealth which he did so much to
produce at home, then he hoped he would be
asiisted by such meetings to secure a happier exist-
enact el owhore. (Cheers.)
Archbishop Manning moved the first resolu-
tion:—

That this meeting 4tceply sympathises with the
agricultural labourers of England in their depressed

circumstances, believing their present position to
be a disgrace in this Pge of civilization, and ini-
mical to the best interests of the country, and is
of opinion that measures should be adopted without
delay for their social improvement and intellectual
elevation.

He readily consented to be present at the meet-
ing, because he believed that there was good cause
-why such a movement as this should be supported,
and because he was given to understand that those
who had taken part in it were actuated by the
most laudable motives. From his own knowledge
of the agricultural labouring classes he fully be-
lieved that their condition was capable of much
improvement, and that, in fact, as the resolution
said, it behoved all who had the good name of
England at heart to see that something was done
to enable that class of persons to set about improv-
ing themselves, both socially and intellectually.
He considered that Parliament had much in its
power which it might do in this direction. (Hear,
hear, and cheers.)
Mr. Thos. Hughes, M.P., regretted the absence
of Canon Girdlestone, whose place he filled, in
seconding a resolution in every word of which he
most cordially agreed. After what they had
heard, could any man doubt the necessity of this
question being discussed, or that it was a disgrace
to our civilization that such men as Mr. Arch, Mr.
Mitchell, and Mr. Ball should toil as they had de-
scribed, and not bo able to earn money enough to
buy proper food ? If all they had heard was true,
the condition of tbo agricultural labour class
was dangerous to the best interests of the country;
and he believed they had adopted the best measure
for their own emancipation in learning to stand
together. Since England had had a history, such
of her citizens as had learned the value of union
had never had to wait long for their rights, and he
did not believe the agricultural labourers, now they
cad learnt to combine, were going to wait much
longer. They would soon be able to got the fran-
chise, and with that in their bands and their union
at their back they would soon do for themselves
what no one else coul do for them, and make their
countrymen proud of them, instead of being as
they were now rather ashamed of them.
(Cheers.)
Sir Charles Trevelyan briefly supported the re-
solution.

Mr. Bradlaugh here made his appearance, and
there was a disturbance at onco, many calling on
him to speak, and others insisting on his sitting
down and allowing the order of proceedings to go
on.

The Chairman put it to the meeting Whether
they would allow Mr. Braillaugh to propose an
addition to the resolution, and, after a confusion of
"Noes" and "Yes" asked them to hoar the
addendum, which
Mr. Bradlaugh then read as follows :
And that there can be no permanent improve-
ment in the condition of the agricultural labourers
until there was a vital change in the land laws, so
as to give to the people their rightful part in the
land.

Ha said: At the instance of the chairman, and
considering the late hour, he would forego his
right to speak, and allow his amendment, if it was
seconded, to be put.
Both the addendum and resolution was then
carried.

Mr. Mundella said at that hour of the night, if
be had had any speech to make, he simuld abandon
it, es there were two resolutions yet to come, and
he did not know what amendments might be pro-
posed ; but he hoped that the meeting would not
defeat the object of those who had convened it.
The resolution he had to move was :

That this meeting congratulates . the farm
labourers on the formation of their Association,
regrading it as the best means of securing an
improvement in their general oondit ion and pros-
pects, a proper interchange of information
affecting the labour market, and a suitable organi-
zation for assisting them in exceptional cases.

It was commonly said that union might he all
well enough for artisans, but there was no neces-
sity for the agricultural labourers to combine.
They had herd - that night that there was cause
enough for them to combine, and they knew that
the result of the combination which they had
carried out, imperfect its it was, was that their
wages had been raised through the whole country.
Parliament, he knew, could not pass a law to pay
them higher wages, but it could pass laws which
would take away the obstructions which now
prevented the farmers from applying capital to
the land. He confessed he had sonic sympathy
with the addendum to the last resolution, but he
should have been glad if it had not been added,
•because he wished to see harmonious action in
this matter. The labouring men must help them-
selves. Association would bring about a better
distribution of labour than there was at present.
Ro was not going to condemn all the landlords ;
hundreds of them had done their duty. But why
should not the Dorsetahire man be put on an equal

footing with the Northumberland man ? It
could be done only by association; he would not
say by strikes—for a strike was the last thing
that should be resorted to—but by association,
and by a proper distribution of labour.
Mr. Daniel Guile seconded the resolution. Forty
years of union had shown him its value, and be
should therefore advise the agricultural labourers
to extend their union. God helped those who
helped themselves. It' they were properly united
they would need no help from outsiders. He
earnestly pleaded for union, and eloquently urged
he labourers' cause.

Sir Charles Mike, who was rapturously ap-
plauded, proposed the next resolution—
That, in order to help the agricultural labourers
in all legitimate efforts for the amelioration of their
depressed condition, this meeting is of opinion
that steps should be taken to procure subscriptions
in aid of the objects set out in the foregoing
resolutim, such subscriptions to be sent to Mr. G.
Mitchell, and to be deposited in the names of the
trustees of the Labourers' Union—Mr. Jesse
Collens, Birmingham; Mr. Edward Jenkins,
London ; Mr. A. Arnold, Hampton-on-Arden;
and Mr. G. W. Ward, Perriston Towers.
Warmly eulogising the speeches made by Mr.
Arch and his fellow-labourers, the hon. gentleman
said he agreed that one of the strongest reasons of
the lamentable condition of the labourers was their
divorce from the soil. Two centuries since half
the soil of England was common soil, but that had
been filched from the labourers, and that had been
the most fruitful source of their degradation. As
to the remedies proposed, ho agreed with those in
the first resolution, and also in the addendum of
Mr. Bradlaugh, though he regretted it had been
mooted for discussion on the occasion. He feared
that the suggestions of Archbishop Manning were
wholly inadequate for the purpose. What they
must look to was giving the labourers power to
raise themselves. The union was doing some-
thing, but they still required help from outside;
and he trusted that would not be relaxed until, in
the prophetic words of William Cobbett, when
next, they were visited, "I hope I may find every
man with a bit of meat upon his table." (Cheers.)
Sir J. Bennett, in seconding the resolution, said
this was the first great meeting in London on this
subject, but it would not be the last. Our land
laws, and game laws, and other laws affecting the
land could not be settled without much discussion
and many meetings. (Applause.)
The Chairman briefly but earnestly appealed to
the meeting to show their practical sympathy with
the agricultural labourers by liberal subscriptions.
The resolution having been carried amidst accla-
mation,

Mr. Taylor, Secretary to the Union, moved a
vote of thanks to the Chairman, stating that the

articles.title: MEETING AT YEOVIL.
articles.text:
MEETING AT YEOVIL.

The Agricultural Labourers' Meeting held at tho
Coin Exchange, on Friday night, was attended by
several hundred persons, every corner of the largo
room being crowded.

Mr. George Potter occupied the chair, and spoke
on the bad condition of labourers' dwellings and
the insufficiency of their wages, urging them to
join the union. He was followed by Mr. George
Mitchell, of Brompton, "a native,of Montacute,
Somerset," who gave numerous particulars ruspeet-
ing the condition of the labouring classes in the
county, and commented in a sarcastic vein on the
kind cf food which fell to their lot. He also spoke
of the rapid spread of the principles inculcated by
the advocates of unionism, and said that within a
short time there would be five hundred members
connected with the Montacute branch. Mr. J.
Mitchell, of Lyme Regis, dilated upon the treat-
ment of labourers when they had to appeal to the
parish for relief. Mr. Arch, President of the
Labourers' Union, and Mr. Allington, a delegate
from Warwickshire, also urged the labourers to
join together for the purpose of obtaining the
justice which had tso long been withhold from them.
During the early part of the proceedings there was
considerable disturbance. Some firmers ventured
to give expression to their disapproval of the
remarks of the speakers, and were forcibly ejected.
There were several exchunations Of dissent after
this, but no disturbance. Towards the close the
chairman called attention to Lord Shafteshury'e
letter, and to the articles in the Builder on the
condition of labourers' dwellings in Somerset.
The following resolution was adopted :
That this meeting is of opinion that the best
means for the agricultural labourers to adopt in
order to obtain a fair remuneration for their labour

is, by the formation of a general union throughout
the country ; and this meeting congratulatts the
Labourers Union that steps have already been
taken to accomplish that object.

at Notiingham have determined to afford the re-
mainder substantial assistance in their struggle

left Dorchester and Bridport for Liverpool, e» route

articles.title: BRADFORD STONE MASONS.
articles.text:
BRADFORD STONE MASONS.

A meeting of the operative masons of Bradford
W5B held on Monday night in the Temperance Hall,
for the purpoec of passing certain resolutioss in
connection with trades union matters, and of pre-
senting, in accordance with the rules of their
society, the SUM of XoD to Nathaniel Wait, one of
the members, who has been disabled by a stroke
of paralysis, from folowing his omploymont as a
mason. The Mayor (Mr. M. W. Thompson)
presided.
Mr. Mark Shepherd moved the first resolution,
which was as follows :

That in the opinion of this meeting, the Friendly
Society of Operative Masons is founded upon
justice, sanctioned by reason and vindicated by
experience, inasmuch as its objects are, the pro-
tection and elevation of its members, the ameliora-
tion of the condition of the working classes
generally, and of the public in particular; as it
provides for sickness, accident, and the relief of
the unemployed, as also the decent interment of
deceased members, their wives and children.
The resolution was seconded by Mr. Charles,
supported by other speakers, and unanimously
carried.

Mr. Cr. Parks proposed tho second Ica 'lotion,
which was :

That in the opinion of this meeting, the criminal
clauses in the recent Trades Union Bill are a one-
sided piece of legislation, and demand the serious
consideration of all trades unionists for the total
repeal thereof.
Mr. Joseph Rae, who seconded the motion, held
that the 6th clause was unfair, in that it made it
illegal for workmen on strike to explain to other
workmen who might come from a distance to take
their places the grievances which had led to the
strike. He deprecated the use of violence or force,
which he thought it was right to punish; but held
it unjust and unfair to prevent
peaceable explana-
tion from being made.
Mr. James supported the resolution, which was
also carried unanimously.
Mr. David Whitehead next presented Mr.
Nathaniel Watt, the disabled member, with £5O,
the sum he was entitled to according to the rules
of the society, and in the course of his remarks
referred, as the other speakers had done, to the
advantages of membership.
A letter of acknowledgment from the recipient
who, from an impediment of speech caused by the
paralysis, was unable to reply orally, was then
read, after which

The Mayor m tde an excellent speech on the
usefulness of trades unions.

THE LONDON CARPENTERS.

IMPORTANT MEETING OF TRADE DELEGATES._

A fully-attended meeting of delegates from the
carious carpenters' societies' shops and jobs, con-

measures necessary to be taken in consequence of
some of the employers having repudiated the

The Chairman, in openin; the proceedings, said

so that

Other employers had refused to pay the extra pay-

Two representative cases on these points would be

(Hear, hear.)
Mr. Stockdale, of the Friends of Freedom

articles.title: SHIP JOINERS OF THE
articles.text:
THE SHIP JOINERS OF THE

THAMES.

About three months since the ship joiners em-
ployed by Mr. Green, the eminent ship builder on
the river Thames, applied to that gentleman for
an advance in the rate of wages, and received for
answer that be thought they were entitled to an
advance, and be was preparad to concede it pro-
vided it was made general amongst all the em-
ployers. Since then the question has undergone
considerable agitation in the trade, and a committee
was appointed to organize a movement for a general
advance of wages. Under the auspices of this
committee an aggregate meeting of the ship
joiners employed on both sides of the river Thames
was held on Saturday at the Sun and Sawyer's
Club Room, High-street, Poplar, when the follow-
ing memorial was submitted, adopted, an ordered
to be sent to the whole of the employers :
Gentlemen,—We, the joiners in your employ,
respectfully solicit your consideration of our pre-
sent position; we are now in a worse social con-
dition than we have been in for a very long time.
The cost of living (as you are aware) has in-
creased at least 30 per cent., while our wages have
remained unaltered, we not having obtained an
increase of pay for over 20 years. We therefore
solicit you to increase our wages 6d. per day on
and after January Ist, 1873. We also ask you to
be so kind as to reply to this memorial as above on
or before December 18th. By acceding to our re-
quest you will retain the willing services of your
best men, who would otherwise be compelled to
leave your employ in quest of better pay else-
where.—On behalf of the Committee,
SAMUEL Wruas, Secretary.

The meeting was then adjourned until the 20th
of December to hear the reply of the employers.

In this month's report Mr. Guile says :—lt will

again an increase on the donation fund this month

amount of cash in band on November 30th,

we hope we aro not yet at the summit of our

prosperity. No doubt a good deal of this con-
tinued prosperity arises from the unity and good
feeling there is amongst ourselves, as well as the
amicable arrangements which exist between us
and our employers. Let it be our constant aim
to keep up these agreeable relationships, and though
we may not attain all we could desire, yet we
shall be able to obtain a good many things which
are worth having, and which will in the future
help us to build up our superstructure upon a
solid and lasting foundation; and accomplishing
this, some of us will have the comfortable know-
ledge when we come to die that we leave the
world better than we found it.

Parliament.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS
AND THE "TIMES."
To the Editor of the BEE-Hivz.'
Sra,—lt would appear as though we wore
guilty of inhuman apathy if we had nothing
to say in reply to the leader of Wednesday in
the Times.
This great oracle can find nothing to say in
a leader occupying more than a column of
print. We characterise it as nothing, because
it is absolutely worse than nothing. The
gobbling of the turkey or the screaming of the
goose would have been more to the purpose,
save and except the concluding sentence,
viz.
"If we would have an abiding improvement
we must be more thorough in our eyamination
of the causes of the degradation we lament,
even if our study leads us to the science of
political economy, which Archbishop Manning
dislikes."
Well, where are these causes to be found P
These causes of degradation are to be found in
the fiscal laws of our country, which not only
rob the labourer of one-third of his wages, but
also deprive his employer of that profit which

munerate the labourer with a more liberal

cut, if not altogether off, very nearly so; so

sinfulness of restricting by legal statute that
which nature sends for the good of all. •

SATURDAY, DECENIBER 11, 1872.

THE CLAIMS 01"rHE FARM
LABOURER.

SOME regions of the earth are obviously far
more fertile than the rest. Even, however, in
the richest soils and under the most favouring
skies, so much of the curse provoked by the
disobedience of the father of our race remains
in force, as makes the sweat of the face an
inexorable condition of eating bread. But
then, in spite of the general worthlessness and
obstructiveness of the spontaneous vegetable
growths,—thorns, thistles, and other weeds,
rank and luxuriant, perhaps, in proportion to
the natural productiveness of different soils
and climes,—in spite of all this, though man
was to eat of the fruit of his own labours and
to eat of it in sorrow, he was to eat of it, he
was to eat bread, and he was so to eat all the
days of/us life.
The inequalities of human condition are a
fact recognized on the same authority by
which these accounts of the effect of evil
among men have come down to us; and we
are admonished as to the heavy and not to ho
shifted responsibilities under which they lay
such as have been more fortunate than the
multitude of their fellow-men in the com-
petitions of life. Appeals are made to the
impartiality and placability of Divine
Providence ; by which sun and rain come to
all alike, whether just or unjust, good or evil,
thankful or unthankful. Those, too, among
us to whom more has come than to others, are
distinctly admonished that to love our
neighbours as ourselves (all men being in this
sense neighbours one to another, though most
of all such as are nearest at hand,) is as bind-
ing a duty as to love the Maker and Preserver
of us all. Besides this, special directions are
given, by obedience to which the incidental
inequalities of condition would be so far toned
down as to preclude from positive want all but
the arrantly idle and worthless for whom,
nevertheless, society makes a provision which,
in workhouses and even in prisons, altogether
stops the downward course of such incor-
rigibles from ending in absolute starvation.
If, in fact, wilful and selfish men would
allow the ALMIGHTY to have his way, (who,
being Almighty, will have it in the end,)
that very labour which was the only curse
caused by sin, would be to mankind the
greatest and a universal blessing. We see
the benevolence of his relenting intentions in
many things; such, for example, as the
regular succession of the seasons, and the
good return to man's labour yielded by the
earth, not simply in the variety and abund-
ance of its available products, but most re-
markably in the wonderfully improved charac-
ter of nearly all of them, as the direct result
of human skill and industry in conjunction
with the inherent powers of earth and sky. Is
it or is it not worth while to spend skill,
money, and toil upon corn-fields and vine-
yards? It surely is, or such enterprizes would
have been abandoned long before now. But
we are not left to mere logical inference. The
fact of the matter lies before us all ; the only
doubt being, whether, in the most cultivable
, and best cultivated regions of the globe, the
highest point of possible agriculture has ever
yet been reached. At the other end of the scale,
we have evidence even more striking. While
fruitful soils are " tickled" into the rendering
of rich harvests, barren wastes are compelled
to afford fruits of increase. On this small and
crowded island of ours, as is admitted by
witnesses the farthest removed from complain-
ing parties, twice as much labour might be
well employed and well paid for, with at least
a duplication of the net result.
What, then, is our actual position in this
matter? Let the agricultural labourers from
Lincolnshire, Someraetshire, and Warwick-
shire, who "spoke their experience" in Exeter
If a 11 on Tuesday night, answer the question.

More generally, however, the state of the case
is this. The surface of Great Britain is divi-
sible into three portions or kinds: that which
is under cultivation, that which is lying waste,
and that which is under taboo to the spade
and the plough. With respect to the middle
portion, though it would be madness to begin
with laying out money and labour upon the
top of the mountain or the moor, yet experi-
ence has amply proved, that land which, from
situation or character, or from both, was once
supposed to be not worth cultivating, may, by
roads, drainage, filth, and toil, be made to
yield some thirty, some sixty, and some even
an hundred fold, as witness the Lothians of
Scotland and the Fens of Lincolnshire. So
long, therefore, as the poor man's alternative
cruelly lies between starvation and emigration,
the gradual and judicious reclaiming and cul-
tivation of the wastes of England must never
cease to be urged upon the lords of manors (as
they are styled) and the Legislature.
The third portion or kind of land, being, for
the most part, rich as well as lying idle, con-
stitutes the ground of a still more powerful
claim upon all who can influence opinion and
impel decision. We have in our eye pleasure-
grounds, parks, game-preserves, and estates in
the hands of corporations and other bodies of
men. At present there is no disposition to
press very hard upon the individual land-
owner. Were every reform demanded by either
tenant-occupiers or farm-labourers, granted
and put in force to-morrow, the pleasures and
conveniences of a country life, as enjoyed by
those of the gentry who spend their whole time
or a part of it on their estates, would neither
be diminished in variety nor decreased in
amount. On the contrary, they would be
mightily enhanced, in every fair and generous
nature, by exemption from fretting cases which
now annoy them, and by the accession of that
crowning comfort, the happy consciousness of
making a largo contribution to the welfare of
their neighbours, at a small, if any, cost or
sacrifice to themselves.

But what is to be said respecting that por-
tion of the soil of England which is under
cultivation from the first of January to the
thirty-first of December? By all means, lot
the owner of the soil, whether private citizen,
public company, or the State and Nation
themselves, enjoy a fair share (whatever that
may be) of the fruits of the earth. By all
means, likewise, let the occupant who expends
his capital upon the fructification of the soil,
reap a proportionate return, and be liberally
considered as to the claim which he has thus
established upon the increased value given to
the farm. Let this, too, be done, so much of
which remains to be even begun, and is even
rosistod with that dogged determination which
springs from a monstrously exaggerated notion
of the rights of property; nay, from a total mis-
conception of their very origin, nature, and ex-
tent. But a third claim, higher and more sacred
than either of the former, than both put to-
gether, is now at last solemnly put in, and
insists upon being considered. We moan that
of the real husbandman, the actual agricul-
tural labourer, him upon the work of whose
hands, and the sweat of whose face, the
production of a harvest, next to the GOD who
made and keeps us all, most immediately and
most principally depends. In a country
called Christian, there ought to be no in-
separable difficulty in settling all those ques-
tions, among the three parties concerned, in
mutual harmony and with reciprocal advan-
tage. If not, the decision must go by
majority; and we suppose that nobody is in
doubt, bow that majority.will ultimately shape
itself. The land-owner and the land-occupier
have long enough seemed to be in a majority
against the solitary labourer. But it must
not, it ought not, it shall not be always so.
Nobody knows better than JOSEIII ARM that
the farmers of the present generation are not
all mere animals, with "brainless heads."
Many, perhaps most of them are grown to be
men of capital in both skull and purse. The
presence of representatives of their own order
in the House of Commons, is convincing the
landlords that they must conform themselves
in all things to the advanced state of opinion
and foeling. Let the agricultural oottiers have
a vote; and it will not be long before they also
find the moue of sending up to that Assembly

men sprung from their own ranks. Three
great counties have already shown us what
they can produce in this kind of growth. The
fields are more favourable to close and deep
meditation than many among us imagine. The
Bishop of MANCTIESTER'S description of what
goes to make an accomplished farm-labourer
ought to be printed as a tract for general dis-
tribution among all other classes. The poet
GRAY, like many another prophet, spoke more
predietively than he was conscious of, when
he sang of the "village 11111PDENS " lying in
the "Country Churchyard." in the grave,
there is neither compliint nor thanksgiving.
But, though from that sleep there will be no
waking till the day of general resurrection, the
peasantry of England are now rousing them-
selves from a long and almost hopeless
torpor; and, we believe and trust, they wil
never rest till they have vindicated the claim
put in for them by a man whom Bishop
ELLICOTT, at any rate, ought to bow to, when
in hourly expectation of martyr4om by the
myrmidons of Nano, "The husbandman
that laboureth must be first partaker of the
fruits."

articles.title: REPRESENTATION OF LABOUR IN
articles.text:
REPRESENTATION OF LABOUR IN

PARLIAMENT.

THE direct representation of labour in Par-
liament is again taking its place among the
questions of tho day. The working classes
arc summoned to combine on this one point.
The House of Commons is still the rich man's
house; the artizans have been dcluded with
promised reforms ; the changes they most
desire are neglected and unduly deferred,
whilst measures affecting the welfare of the
wealthy classes are constantly studied and
actively promoted ; and the workers of the
country are an excluded class in the law-
making council of the nation.
To further the movement, a conference of
delegates and representatives of trade and
industrial associations was hold on Monday, at
the Town Hall, Birmingham. The conference,
which was convened by the London and Bir-
mingham Labour Representation League, was
presided over by Mr. It. M. LATILtat, Presi-
dent of the London Labour Representation
League, and delegates were present from
various parts of the country.
The CHAIRMAN, in his opening address,
dwelt upon the necessity of direct labour re-
presentation, and said the object of the meet-
ing was to determine upon the steps to be
taken to secure the return to Parliament at
the next general election of men who would
represent the various industries of the country.
Papers were read on "Organisation of Labour
for Seouri ng its Direct Representation," "Com-
plete Electoral Reform," and the neeessity of
relieving candidates from electoral expenses.
Resolutions were passed to the effect that the
time had arrived for organisation to secure
direct representation of labour in the House
of Commons; protesting against the House of
Commons refusing to relieve candidates from
the expenses of elections, and recommending
the formation of a national fund, by subscrip-
tions, for the purpose of defraying such costs
for working class candidates at the next
general election; and strongly urging upon
the Government the necessity of re-arranging
constituencies so that a fair system of propor-
tionate representation should be formed, and
pledging the meeting to support such measures
of political reform as should ensure a perfect
system of equal franchise for county and
borough, equal voting for every elector, and a
wider choice in the selection of candidates.

A public meeting was held in the evening,
when the resolutions adopted by the Con-
ference were formally approved.

A report of the proceedings will be found in
another column.

articles.title: CIVIL SERVICE STORE ATTACKED.
articles.text:
THE CIVIL SERVICE STORE
ATTACKED.

THE shop-keeping world has set about the
organization of its strength with the view of
doing battle against co-operation. The meet-
ing ia Willis's Rooms the other evening was
crowded and enthusiastic. THOMAS CRAM--
BERS, M.P. for Marylebone, presided, and
Alderman McArrutm, M.P. for Lambeth,
moved the first resolution, whilst several other
members of Parliament wrote sympathizing
letters of apology for not being present.

The position for members of Parliament on
any contest that may arise on this subject
cannot but be very painful and puzzling.
Our representatives, like other men, possess
honest convictions on a certain number of
public) questions, but unfortunately they have
to make their minds up end take sides on
many questions of which they know little
or nothing, and as it certain number of
votes hang upon any decision they may come
to, negatively or affirmatively, it must be a
difficult thing sometimes to balance loss and
gain when a decision on some exciting ques-
tion is suddenly called for.

This co-operative question is not one to be
easily settled by the ordinary member of Par-
liament mind, as it has never yet been made
a question for the hustings. The shop-keepers
do not understand it; their anger against it
clouds a judgment never particularly pene-
trating or comprehensive, except in pursuing
the interest of the till. So far, as a perusa lof
the speeches at Willis's Rooms proves, they
arc utterly at sea in dealing with the question
they have taken in lattud. They arc savage
with the Civil Service Association, and angry
with co-operation generally, but they do not
understand the diffirenoe between the two,
and miss their aim by dividing their atten-
tion, and therefore deliver their blows whore
they can have no effect.

They see that a huge business, organized
by the Civil servants of the Crown, has
grown up at their doors, and they are going
to move the Government with a view to its
suppression, by asking to have the Civil ser-
vants prohibited from engaging in such con-
cerns. These men, with their members of
Parliament at their head, are insane enough
to think that a " huge " business which has
grown in a most unprecedented manner will
be given up at the call of the Administration ;
that Civil servants, trembling for their safety,
will cease to buy and selilu their now fashion,
and run to the shops of the ordinary traders
to pay an extra 20 per cent. for what they
want, that their proprietors may pocket the
profit, and become smoothed into mildness.
We cannot say what the House of Commons
or what the Government may do under such a
pressure as the shopkeepers will put upon
thorn. They may try to interfere with the
Civil servants, even so far as to refuse them
the right of association for any purpose what-
ever. They may even force them to buy their
watches of Mr. JONES, in the Strand, and
pledge them at some one of Mr. ATTEN-.
BOROUGR'S numerous pawnshops. What a
Government under pressure may do, it is very
difficult to say.
But it must not be forgotten that there is a
remedy for every evil, and nothing would be
more easy than to have these establishments
carried on, and their custom' continued under
a name and in a way with which these irritated
retailers could not interfere. If the business is
an advantage to those who carry it on and
deal in it, no amount of scolding will put it
down, even when indulged in under the
patronage of a few common-place metropo-
litan members of Parliament, who, unhappily
for themselves, hold their seats on the simple
condition of pleasing the shopkeepers, .great
and small, whose premises line our thorough-
fares, and who cannot possibly continue to
exist except on the profit they make by buying
their commodities at one priori, and selling
them at another. If, however, their success
was as complete as they wish in their campaign
against the Civil Service—what then? The
Civil Service Stores in London are but a young
growth of co-operation, and it is right to add that
they are not a quite legitimate growth, though
it is the true Co-operator, not the shopkeeep or,
who has any right to complain of it. If it
cheapen distribution it is a gain to the com-
munity, but if it does not affect this in the
best way, which is what the true Co-operator
insists on; it is, therefore, a partial betrayal of
a principle which in its operation at every stop
benefits the general commun.ity in many ways
besides those of cheapness and honesty of
1 dealing.

Mr. LEwis, of Cardiff, declared that the
co-operative system was destructive of !‘ tra-
ding morality." We were always under the
impression that the shopkeepers themselves
WO done that tong ago, and that co-operatioN

was regarded as a means of restoring it,
by uniting the interests of the buyer and
seller. But it would appear, according to Mr.
/AMU, that when a customer gets back money
by showing a ticket of membership, morality
is destroyed. The manner in vogue amongst
shopkeepers is different to this. They give
discounts and bribes to servants, and compen-
sate themselves by a little manipulation in
counting, weighing, or measuring; practices,
which, no doubt, square very well with a
shopkeepers notions of commercial morality.

171105LkS CHAMBERS, M.P., has a bad
case in hand. Alderman MclaTuun has got
into a fog in which he may lose himself.
They are lending themselves to a shabby cru-
sade, in which the whole spirit and tendency
of the times are against them. The hundreds
of thousands of working men who have en-
tered into the co-operative business, and who
feel daily the value of the services they are
conferring on themselves and others, are not
to be frightened from their task by the
alarmed screaming of angry retailers, or the
ignurant denunciation of subservient members
of Parliament. If they think co-opera-
flan must inevitably lead to a " war of classes,"
as Mr. CUAMBERS stated, then that war of
classes must come, as no honcst co-operator
wcuid, ever think of abandoning the good work
mien which he has entered to avoid a collision
with the shopkeepers of the country, even
though when led by so doughty a soldier as
Mr. LIMAS CHAMBERS, M.P. for Marylebone.

articles.title: APPROACHING DISSOLUTION IN
articles.text:
THE APPROACHING DISSOLUTION IN

FRANCE.

Tax situation of things in France is im-
proved. Not that the Royalist factions, or,
rather, the anti-Republican League, have re-
laxed, in their purpose to prevent, if possible, the
establishment of a government without a
monarch; but that they are not proceeding
with that precipitancy which seemed, at one
time, to be driving thorn upon a headlong and
reckless course. The chief of the clerical
party, Monsignor DIIPANLOUP, has, for ono,
been made to see, that, even in an Assembly the
majority of which is reactionist, he cannot
have his way against a Minister so little to
the taste of his order as M. JULES &moist.
The badgerings to which he is put by men of
the Right, either recoil upon themselves, or,
as in the case of the. pictures " abstricted "
under the Empire, rebound with damaging
4ffect upon those strange bedfellows, the
Bonapartists, with whom the misery of the
Legitimists is making them acquainted. One
Of these country gentlemen who made an in-
effectual attempt to cut down the allowances
to the opera and the theatres of Paris, grounded
his objection upon a reason which shows the
revival of the old antipathy betwixt country
and town. "Why," he asked, "should the
P4:1410111ta of the South pay to support dancers,
singers, and actors, whom they never saw or
heard?"

In the mean time, M. TRIERS pursues the
even tenour of his way. The changes made
among his Ministers, instead of signifying any
eompromise with the majority of the Assembly,
intimate rather a hope on his part that'the
oscillation hown in some of its votes may be
determined the other way. M. CA:TALON, for
instance, was too Republican for the Rurais,
who, therefore, wore glad to 080 him leave the
lime Office, but his translation to the Pre-
feeture of the Seine, where he has more iin-
portance as well as better pay, has simply
afforded him the opportunity, in entering
upon the new office, of proclaiming the Re-
public to be "a necessity of the times."
Moreover, the place vacated in the office of
the Interior has been filled by a gentleman
(M. FOUILNIER) whose little finger, in point of
Republieanism, is reported to be thicker than
M. Ctamores loins. The election of the Duke
la BROGLIE, by the single vote of the Prince
bE JOINVILLE, upon the Committee of Thirty,
la place of M. DE Fourotr, who has been made
Minister, 'is ground for believing that M.
Turns* is regarded as irretrievably committed
to the Republic, for the DUKE Is notoriously
averse from him, and. the PRINCE has made it
evident that, though his family have returned
feem exile and got back their property
through his infin,ence, this is all that they ex-
pect from hire. As for the French people*

they clearly perceive that these Princes, who
have more care for themselves than for their
country, are the true descendants of Monsieur
JOHN SMITH, alias King Louts PltturrE.

But the greatest indication of coming events
is in those shadows cast before, the petitions
for a Dissolution. These thicken the air like
snow -flakes. While the local authorities
appear to beat them back, they only come
down the more and drift with increased force.
Any one may see that, so long as M. Limns
and his administration cannot be convicted of
causing them, they are quite welcome to en-
velope the theatre of Versailles. 130 this as
it may, the Dissolution movement makes long
and rapid strides. The Moderates and the
Republicans of the Left are openly agreed.
The subject is to be debated in the Assembly
this day. A Royalist moved for leave to bring
it on, his purpose being to crush the petitions.
M. GAMBETTA. promptly took up the glove,
seconding the motion, and, in doing so, de-
clared his longing and readiness for an imme-
diate, direct, and thorough debate. We do
not venture to affirm a mutually avowed under-
standing between M. Tnuns and M. Gim-
BETTA. ; but we see in the coming debate a
confirmation of our formerly expressed views
of the masterly conduct of the latter; and we
now venture to predict, as the inevitable result,
whatever the immediate veto may be, the dis-
solution, or, what would be practically the
same thing, the supercession of the present
Assembly.

THE EARL OF, SHREWSBURY AND
THE FARM LABOURERS.

NOTHING could be better than the spirit ex-
hibited by the .Earl of SHREWSBURY when
addressing his tenants a few days since on his
Worcestershire estates. The EARL wishes to
do the best he can for his tenants, and he is
anxious that his tenants should be liberal and
kindly to their labourers. He considers the
labourers should have better cottages, and
personally he is exerting himself to supply
them. He has also raised his own labourers
and gardeners from 138, to 155.. per week.
What his farmers give he does not mention,
and he suggests that the work of the men
should be made as easy as possible on Sundays
that they may attend church or chapel.
These are the Emit's own words as given
in the newspapers, and we presume that the
15s. per week, with better cottages than they
now have, and a little more leisure on Sundays
to be devoted to the chtirch pr the chapel,
would be the Earl of SHREWSBURY'S notion of
the leisure and abundance of a golden ago in
the farming districts of. England. Vew
fashioned things like Chambers of Agriculture
he does not like, and probably his prejudices
would run as strongly against the abolition of
the old smock frock and clouted shoes of poor
Flom E.

We shall leave it to those who are strong
In figures to say how 15s. ought to be laid out
to bring most comfort to the homes, of the
labourers, a problem which will probably be
explained by the time his lordship's farmers
have followed his liberal example in regard to
the wages of the poor fellows who have the
misfortune to work for a tenant instead of a
landlord. It is quite clear, however, that the
atm does not expect his tenants to do very
mush in this way, as after four years' farming
by himself, the Accounts of which were very
accurately kept, he was £3O out of pocket. Of
course, the noble EA.ltt, may be a very good land-
lord, and, at the same time, a very bad farmer.
As, however, he does not go into details,
nothing can bo accurately stated on this head.
It is quite clear, however, that oven at 15s.
per week the labourer has too little rather
than too rau3ll wages, and if any alte-
ration is to be effected to enable the farmers
to make both ends meet, it ought to be by a
reduction in rent, or by an enhancement of
the price of farm produce, and it is pretty clear
that the public are quite satisfied that the
price of farm produce is high enough already.
However, his lordship and other great land
owners, have it quite in their power to relieve
the fanners in this matter, even though the
labourers should insist on 20s. per week-a not
very extravagant sum, when the wants of a
family at present cost of provisions have to be
considered.

The only thing which neemed to disturb the

equanimity of the Earl of SHREWSBURY was
the wickedness of the "agitators," who go
about "setting class against class." What is
the reason somebody does not catch these
"agitators," and lay them by the heels?
Those who have seen them, ought to describe
them, that they may be put into the" hue and
cry," and apprehended when met with. They
must have " saucer " eyes, cloven feet, and
clawed hands. When they breathe it cannot
be anything less than flame. They madden
the labourer, and make him discontented
with his position. How could he else ex-
pect more than ten shillings a week, or
desire anything better than a brute's life and
a pauper's death?
Seriously, does the Earl of SHREWSBURY
think people are fools ? Does he suppose that
he and others like him can preserve the pre-
sent accursed condition of things by abusing
"agitators ?" Or does he for a moment
imagine that the country will allow itself to be,
dragged in the direction of anarchy and ruin
by the misery and madness of its agrieutural
labourers, that he and others like hint may
outshine in splendour the barbaric sovereigns
of the East? The account between landlords,
tenants, and labourers will have to be squared
in a much more satisfactory way than at pre-
sent, and that speedily too, or our great land-
holders may have to suffer far more of a loss
individually by turbulent discontent than the
noble EAnr. did by his four years' farming.
Lord SHREWSBURY seems to be one of the beat
of his kind, bat it may not be wrong to
remind him that such grievances as those of
the English labourers cannot be settled by
benevolent small talk.

articles.text:
MR. W. IT. SAITH,

Mn. W. 11. Surrn, M.P. for Westminster,
has just returned from a visit to America,
and has been " letting himself out" to the
Westminster Working Men's Conservative
Association. His views about the
though somewhat extreme, are neither new
nor important. He thinks it will be the " first
step towards the introduction of corruption to
a larger extent, and in a more organized
manner than has ever been known in the
history of English elections." This is a strong
statement, and leads us to the belief that
either Mr. SMITIt is on the look-out for some-
thing perfectly horrible in regard to our
future elections, or that his knowledge of our
past electioneering struggles is not of a very
accurate or extensive kind. But the hon.
gentleman fortifies himself by experience
gleaned during his visit to America. He has
been in the booths and seen the votes de-
posited, and he has "gathered the opinion of
the Americans themselves, and the impression
left on his mind of what they have sought to
convey is that there is with them a corruption
that is -almost, universal, and that corruption
is not thought to be a dishonourable thing."
We do not say that this is net Mr. Sstern's

he repeated to the 'Westminster Conservative
working men. But after a perusal of the tales
of travellers of all sorts and sizes, we refuse
• to pay much attention to the recitals of the
political Smell-fungusses and Smell-dung,usses
who run to America or elsewhere for the pur-
pose of justifying their foregone conclusions.
There is nothing more puzzling than the
quickness, almost amounting to intuition, by
which these travellers get to know whatever

their inquisitive feet are placed on foreign
soil. Multitudes of them move up and down
their native country for the greater part of
their lives without becoming particularly well

facts connected with their fellow-country-
men. Wo have at this moment every
possible difference of opinion as to the condi-

aristocracy, a manufacture ofeldest sons, or slave

why the matter Should not have been settl°4 •

.of
cannon and thrusting of bayonets. Mr, •

.regard to the requirements of

whenever
,possible for the settlement of

The description given by Mr. S3IITII of the

"interfere

Mr. SMITH is certainly a clever man, and the

MILL. He is clearly a much better repre-

• THE GAS STOKERS' STRIKE.
• ThE issue of the gas etokers' strike cannot
be satisfactory to those who desire to see the
cause of the working men successful on the
side of reason and justice. At the same time
it carries with it a lesson of the highest use
to winking men if they will read it aright and

Working men, to whatever calling they
belong, have two things to discover, and until
they find them out and root them in their
memories, they will never be able to command
the flumes they desire. First, if they decide
on_ arbitration as the best means of settling
the disputes between themselves .and their
employers, and if they mean to obtain satis-
factory awards, they must take care in every
'-
thing they demand or resist to have plain,
honest, obvious justice on their side. 'Without
this precaution, arbitration is about the worst
thing to which they can resort. If they are
determined, as far as they know how, to do
what is right, and desire even their own cor-
rection,—if justice and fairness, as between
employer and employed, require it,—then they
should put themselves in the right, and care-
fully keep themselves there a 4 persistently as
possible.
Secondly, if they depend on strikes—if
a 'fair, honest, open battle is what they re-
quire,—they shoul& organize and discipline
their strength, and rely on it absolutely for
the attainment of their ends. Under any cir-
cumstances, we should counsel organization
and discipline ; and if arbitration, on perfectly
fair terms, cannot he secured, we should
advise hard and resolute fighting by way of
strikes. _ _ _

If fighting an be escaped let it be avoided,
but if it cannot let those who enter on it do
so with all the skill and force a careful prepara-
tion can give them. Now, what we complain
of in regard to recent strikes on the part of
ill-organized bodies, such as railway porters,
the carpenters and joiners, in their recent
strikes, is, that they really were not prepared.
They had neither the necessary organization,
nor adequate funds ? They had no resolute
orderly following, and what is almost worse
even than this, they were entirely with-
out adequate skilled leadership. The whole
thing resembled a blind rush, which under
peculiarly favourable circumstances might lead
to victory, but which in nineteen oases out of
twenty, could only bring discomfiture and
defect.

Comment woull be superfluous in the gas
stokers' case. They have fought the battle
in their own way and lost it, to the satisfaction
of the general public. Wherein, if they had
so managed their business as to have kept the
public on their side, they could scarcely
have failed to win. They ought to
have accepted the discharge of the
men who were treated in the manner
complained of—supported these men by money
grants—and appealed to the public against the
miserable spirit of vindictiveness in which
they were discharged. If they had done this,
they could not have failed in their object;
their Own skill in the management of their
affairs would have carried them through. As
matters stand, nothing satisfactory has been
accomplished, The Union very likely will be
broken up, thousands of pounds will be lost

to the men on strike, and no good will have
been done to any soul alive..
Cannot the organized trades societies set up
a tribunal to which appeal may be made by
working men in all important eases before a
strike takes place ? If such a court of appeal
existed, thousands of pounds would be saved,
and more than this, those blunders which
bring diseredit on trades unionism would be
avoided.
But whilst we condemn much that has been
done by the men, we cannot overlook the pro-
vocation they received, and, above all, we are
bound to condemn the savage manner in which
they are now being hunted down. The magis-
trates, in sending certain of them to prison
with hard labour, may think they are only
vindicating the law; but they are doing this
in such a class spirit as to turn the law into an
injustice and an oppression. It is in the very
nature of things that snail should be the case.
The worker is yet considered a servant.
Gums has got his brass collar off, but be is
yet born thrall to CEDnrc THE SA:tox. Middle
and upper class men everywhere, in private
conversation, in the press and elsewhere,
though they sometimes allow the right of our
workers to combine, in a thousand ways un-
consciously show their hatred of such com-
binations, and so long as the law gives them
the power to work out that hatred in its name,
opportunities will not be allowed to slip for
bringing the severities of prison life to the aid
of authority in the workshop.
We have no hesitation in saying that the
sentences passed on some of the men are out-
rages on justice, and if the working men of
the kingdom allow such shameful conduct to
be continued without a strong protest, they
will richly deserve any stigma it implies, and
if they do not rise up as one man, and demand
that what is simply a civil offence in an em-
ployer shall only be a like offence in them,
much of what they have to say about the
liberty of the citizen, and the rights of labour,
will be mere nonsensical mouthing.
