MOSES AND SON'S AEMINACK.

This pocket diary for 1873 is in every respect
equal to those published the last few years. It
can be obtained at either of Moses and Son's
establishments, or at the bookstalls of the Metro-
politan Railway, and although superior to those
usually sold at sixpence is offered to the public at

Bradford is not exactly the place from which
one would expect to hear an utterance by
Mr. Gathorne Hardy; but he was drawn to
that Radical borough by the consecration of a
church erected in memory of his late brother
Charles; and at the luncheon which followed
the ceremony, replying to the toast of "the
two Houses of Parliament," he reproached the
members of the Legislature for looking more
to local than to imperial questions. He dis-
tinotly refused to abjure party, regarding few
things as more dull and mournful than an
assembly of 658 Englishmen all of one and the
same mind; and while deprecating and dopier-
the divisions in the Church, he asserted for
that Church a special duty, in regard to educa-
tion, the neglect of which might be visited on
her as a national crime.

On Tuesday evening an appalling explosion
of dynamite occurred at St. Austell. Win.
Webb, foreman of the railway works, took
home—contrary to the rules of the company—
twelve cartridges of this powerful explosive,
with the view of drying them for the next day's
blasting operations, lie placed them for this
purpose on a hot plate used for cooking. They
were in the house at the time besides himself,
Webb's wife, his father-in-law, and two chil-
dren sleeping in their cots. Suddenly, with
terrific force, the dynamite exploded, levelling
to the earth all the walls of the house except
two, and scattering everything it had contained
over the fields. Only one of the occupants
was killed instantly, but the others when found
were so dreadfully burnt and crushed that it is
almost impossible they can survive.

articles.title: DIRECT REPRESENTATION OP LABOUR IN PARLIAMENT.
articles.text:
DIRECT REPRESENTATION OP
LABOUR IN PARLIAMENT.

620.111.
•11.0.64

CONFERENCE IN' BIRILINGHAId. —T—
A conference of delegates and representatives ef
crude and industrial societies on the subject of the
direct representation of labour in Parliament, was
held on Monday in the committee-room of the
Town Hall. Mr. R. M. Latham, president of the
London Labour Representation League, occupied
the chair, and amongst those present were Coun-
cillors Austin, Morley, and Cooke; Messrs. Edwin
Seager and W. H. Packwood, Stourbridge ; George
Burridge, George Howell, representatives Reform
Association, London; Daniel Bayley, Birming-
ham; Thomas Mottershead, London ; Alfred W.
Addleton, Henry Giles, John Davison, T. Bint,
J. E. Osborne,. G. H. Reddalls, S. Mills, P. Gor-
ky, G. Bill, Charles Hibbs, Henry Clements,
Birmingham; Charles Williams, general secretary
National Association of Plasterers; Councillor
Akey and James Kithringham, Worcester; T. G.
Facey, London; James Gamwell, IL Broadhurst,
Labour League, London; John Sargeant, Amal-
gamated Society of Railway Servants; A. Walton,
Brecon; John Kane, secretary of National Society
of Ironworkers; and George Potter, London.
The following letters of apology for non-at-
tendance were read by Mr. George Bill :
DEAR SIR, —lt will not he in my power to
attend your proposed conference to be held on the
9th inst. I thank you for your letter of invitation,
and for your kind wish for the restoration of my
health.
I am, very respeotfully yours,
JOIN- BRIG T.
Mr. G. Bill, Racket-court, Bath-street,
Birmingham.
DrAn Stn,—l have to acknowledge the receipt
of your circular in the matter of the Labour
Representation Conference at Birmingham, on the
9th inst., together with the enclosures. Thanking
you for the information forwarded,
I am, yours obediently,
GEonoc DIXON.
DEAR Fra,—ln reply to your note of the 30th
ult., I do not think that it would be possible for
me to attend your proposed meeting, otherwise I
should have liked to leant bow you propose to
carry out your object. There are members of the
House of Commons who have been working men,
but I understand your object to be that men shall
remain working mos and have seats in the House.
This is impracticable, as if a member does his duty
it would be impossible for him to continue to work
as an artisan.
Yours faithfully,
I'. H. MTINTZ.
Mr. G. Bill.

Mr. A. Brogan, M.P., also wrote expressing
his sympathy with the objects of the Labour
Representation League.
The Chairman, in addressing the delegates, said
he was satisfied that nothing but their earnestness
in the cause of labour had brought them together.
It was a cause the advocacy of which had never
been fashionable. They had the gratification of
knowing, however, that. the working classes were
daily growing in str.ength, in self-reliance, and in
that power of organisation by whose aid they must
ultimately overcome all difficulties. Their ad
growth in intelligence and in the knowledge of the
business of life would enable them to exercise
their power, not for the benefit of their Own class
merely, but of every class in the country. But
they maintained that labour, having its own
thought and its own sense of right, should also
have. a voice of its own, and should ingot on higher
justice and fairer treatment for the working man
than he had ever yet received. Without despising
the help of others already in Parliament, their
primary duty was to help themselves. At present
they were scattered, and therefore powerless; but
when united in a common understanding they
would be able to make their power felt. (Applause.)
The great object of the Conference was to consider
what steps should be taken for the return of work-
ing men to Parliament at the next general election.
There were already hon. gentlemen in the House
of Commons doing what they could in the interest
of labour; but, having had no experience of the
worker's life, they could not express with the
same clearness and earnestness the worker's
thoughts, Pre-eminent amongst the questions to
be considered was the desirableness of the working
classes having a distinct policy in regard to the
political and social affairs of the nation. It was as
easy to answer that question as to ask it. No
sane man could doubt that those who lived by
, labour should seek so to direct the current of
public opinion and to shape the laws of the nation
as to secure for labour a more equitable share in
the profits of industry, and, beyond this, So as to
influence the policy of the Government that the
nation might live at peace with its neighbours.
Ho meant by this simply that the masses of the
people should have some definite and understood
policy, whereby peace would be maintained, in-
dustry 'promoted, Itiad the claims of labour duly
° recognised. Those claims must be pressed, and

working men, if need be, should tarn their backs
on members of Parliament who declined to ad-
vance them. Other subjects which demanded
immediate and earnest consideration in the interest
of labour were a revision of the poor-law system
and our extravagant national expenditune and the
consequent heavy taxation of the people. (Ap-
plause.)

Mr. G. H. Reddalls (Birmingham) read a
paper on the Direct Representation of Labour.
He said they were agreed upon the necessity
of obtaining direct representation of labour.
They had now to decide how this object was
to be effaeted. The almost universal failure
of working class candidates for parliamentary,
municipal, and school board honours could be
traced to the want of organization and money.

With regard to organization, there should be a
working man's electoral association in every town.
The active members of the association should be
classified according to the wards in which they re-
sided, and certain portions of each ward assigned
to each member for special canvassing.
,With re-
gard to the finance question, he was sorry to any
that it had been the usual custom of men), work-
ing class political associations to " send rotind the
bat" to the middle-class whenever money Wae
wanted. They must have no more of this. If
they put themselves Under obligation to a clue
which was frequently opposed to their interests,
they could neither be 'consistent nor Preserve their
independence. An electoral fend should 'he °Stab-
fished in connection With each Working Class aiio.
ciation. When the time for actien arrived they
must have no shrinking beck. Mr. O. Dixon,
M.P., at a meeting held last week, Wile kind
enough to say that when this borough returned
eight members they would be able to return one
working man. They would respectfully tell that
gentleman that they were not content to wait Until
then. They thought one, at least, of the three
members which Birmingham returned should be a
representative of the working classes; and they
hoped when the general election came to be pre-
pared with a man. With a strong organization,
an electoral fund, a united party, and a wise party,
success was certain. (Applause.)
Mr. Broadhurst (London) read a paper on the
same subject. They were all agreed its to the im-
portance of organization. Emil branch should
form itself into an agency for promoting the can-
didature of working moo, and communicating the
enquiries they made to a common centre. It was
not necessary for trades unions to vote money for
political purposes which had beim amassed for
trade matters, but he thought trivia unionists
might contribute to a separate fund. Taking the
number of unionists to be 300,000, and the sub.
scription one shilling each, £16,000 would 'be
raised; and that would enable them to carry a
dozen or so of candidates. Tie had spoken of a
common centre. Ile thought they had such a
contra in the Labour Representation League,
Mr. George Howell then read a paper on
" Complete Electoral Reform." I.le said that
electoral reform was at the base of all future pro.
gross. It decided the progress of their, statesmen
and controlled the legislative action of the Cabinet.
They were on the eve of another Reform Bill,
and it was for the people to say how far that bill
should lay down the principles which should be
their guide in the future, and to what extent it
should go. That which they all desired was an
equal representation and equal distribution of
political power. They wanted, Ist, an equal fran.i
chide for county and borough; 2nd, an equal
apportionment
,of members to population; 3rd, the
Widest possible choice in the election of canal.
dates. With regard to the first point, it would be
sufficient for him to say that he meant it, In the
widest
,possible sense of the word, to be' inclusive,
and not exclusive; for with household suffrage ex-
tended to the counties, the muddle of the lodger
franchise as it now was, and the antique character
and obstructiveness of the .Registration Courts,
would be more and more seen, and a cry ,would
arise calling for the abolition of such useless and
eiponsive machinery, the money saved from which
Could be appropriated to the legal enamsee of
elections. In order to secure the principle and
practice of equality in representation it was not
necessary, oven were it desirable, to out up the
whole country into 668 new electoral districts,
each with a population of something under 60,00,0
souls. The whole of the objects sought by the
equal electoral districts of the Charter, and by the
ward plan as suggested by Mr. Cobden, and other
objects also of not loss importance to that Confer-
ence„ could be secured by a less costly, a more
mature, and a simpler and more effective plan.
They took England as she was, with the country

as the unit, and apportioned to each division us
many members as there were quotients pf 4,000
each. But in order that the machinory of the
whole arrangement might be simplified, and also

to preserve to their constituencies that spice of
local interest which often served to give vitality
and earnestness to their elections, they would
retain those large centres of industry in not less
than three quotients, or a population of 150,000,
and give to them their proportion of members.
(Hem., hettr.)

Mr. Mottershead, London, road a paper upon
the same subject. He said that in the old days
of Parliamentary struggle there were large prizes
to be fought for. Government influence meant
family influence, and family influence, with party
politicians, meant family gain. These old contests
wore only open to rich men. In the true accepta-
tion of the word, the " people " were scarcely
considered at all, and their interests and happi-
ness had only such thought as was requisite to
make them and keep them as a great balancing
power, used for the purpose of steadying and
upholding the party in office, or for helping those
who wanted to get there. Ile need not say that
this heavy expenditure at elections prevented con-
stituencies looking for any but rich candidates.
This
,was made quite clear by the fact that the
abolition' of the property qualification did not
bring poor men into the field. After alluding to
the dishonest shifts by witieh the parties attained
their ends, Mr. Mottershead said that they knew
that their Parliament was not composed of
England's wisest, but rather England's richest
men, anxious in many cases to promote special
interests. In the legal profession there were some
who regarded a seat in the House of Commons as
a bench from which to climb to professional honour
and emolument. (Applause.)

Mr. G. If. Reddalls moved :
That in the opinion of this Conference, consider-
ing the probable early dissolution of Parliament ,
the time has arrived for a determined eff )rt to be
rnadeto organise the labouring classes by means
of their various associations, with a view to secure
the direct representation of labour in the House
of Commons.

The resolution was seconded by Mr. J. Osborne,
Birmingham.

Mr. Thomas (Birmingham) said if he misunder-
stood Mr. Reddens, he withdrew the remark.
He had, however, heard it said at other meetings
in the town, and repeatedly said, that the time
had come when they should send a Tory for Bir-
mingham rather than the Liberals they bad here.
He could not endorse this. When they brough t
out a candidate they must bring him out with
some chance of success. He did not believe in
splitting themselves up into fragments for the
purpose of one or two parties getting popularity,
and thus destroying the usefulness of that asso-
ciation. He believed that the working class in
Birmingham might return a candidate at the next
general election if they were united. (Cheers).
• Mr. George Potter, of London, in supporting the
resolution, said they should all understand the
grievance of which they complained. It was that
labour was not represented in the Legislature.
(Cheers). At present the constitution of the House
of Commons was as follows: The fighting interest,
naval and military, had '220 representatives; the
aristocratic interest had 178 representatives ; the
official interest, present ministers and ex-Ministers,
were 86; the agricultural interest had 146 repre-
sentatives; the monetary interest had 21; the
railway interest, 65; the legal interest 107 ; the
literary and scientific, 26; the cotnmereial and
manufacturing, 108; the 7,000,000 of adult labou-
rers and artisans had not one direct representative
In the House of Commons. (Shame.) At the
last election he showed the lodgers in all the great
towns could not exercise the privilege of voting.
At the election of 1868 hundreds and thousands of
lodgers could not vote on account of their names
not being properly placed on the register. He
argued, therefore, that they must endeavour to
secure a good registration bill. He also asked
them to try and get the county franchise assimi-
lated to borough franchise; and if they succeeded
in this they would have the support of 600,000
agricultural labourers. He further suggested they
should got up a demonstration of artisans and
labourers in a dozen large towns some time in
April next, in favour of two distinct objects—the
representation of labour in Parliament, and the
repeal of the Criminal Law Amendment Act.
(Cheers). They were not assembled for the pur-
pose of directing the Liberal party, but they wished
It to go forth from that Conference that the grie-
vance of which they complained was one which the
working men of England would no longer allow
to exist without protesting against it. He pointed
out that if labour was to be directly represented,
they must have a fund subscribed which would be
Indicative that there would be a great agitation.
He thought that when there were two members to
be elected, and the Liberal party would not recog-
nise their claims, they must be united and carry
their man with a plump vote, which would place 1

him at the head of the poll, and then the Liberals
might fight for the other seat. (Applause).
Mr. Dalzell (Birmingham) complained that
they could never get the assistanco of the Liberal
party in the matter of labour zepresentation, and
he asked how it was they were not on that occasion
patronized by the Liberal Association?

Mr. Alfred Walton (Brecon) denied the state-
ment made by some journals that the working
classes were in favour of class legislation. They
did not wish to send a working man to Parliament
simply because he was a working man, but they
insisted upon labour not being excluded.

Mr. Mitten (Birmingham Liberal Association)
advi,ed them not to forsake the Liberals, but to
make use of thorn for their purposes, as the Libeial
party had made use of thorn tor their interests.
He would never support a Tory, and advised them
not to go round to the Tory party, who only
wanted them for their own interests.

Mr Mottershead indignantly denied that the
League were taking the side of the Conservative
party in this matter. He had never voted for a
Conservative and never should. But he said when
they, the Liberal party, forsook them ho should
look to his own interests and take no notice of the
Liberal interest when it was opposed to his. The
Liberal party only sought them for their own in-
terest. Now he had a power for himself he should
use it for his order if he thought proper. If the
Liberal party did not support his class, and he
found their interests against them, be should exer-
cise his discretion with regard to his vote.
Mr. Councillor Airey (of 'Worcester) supported
the resolution, saying that he was opposed when
he came forward as a candidate for the Council of
that city, by a wealthy Liberal. They must not
depend upon the Liberals. They must stick to
their own colleagues, "Who would be free him-
self must strike the blow."
The resolution was then carried.

Mr. John Kane, of Darlington, moved—
That this Conference enters its protest against
the conduct of the Rouse of Commons in refusing
to relieve canilidates from the vexatious official
expenses at elections and recommend the forma-
tion of a national fund by subscription to he placed
in the hands of trustees, for the purpose of defray-
ing such iniquitous cost for working class candi-
dates at the next general election.
He said the various trades unions were c ipit3l
organizations, whereby they might be got at.
Referring to the cry of splitting the Liberal party,
he remarked that he was disposed to work for
neither Whig nor Tory, and should advise working
men not to be the moans of placing men in power
who had treated them in such a scurvy way as
those whom they had supported.

Mr. Broadhurst seconded the resolution, which,
after a short discussion, was carried unani •
mously.
Mr. George Bill moved—
That this Conference, believing that the time
has arrived for the completion of electoral reform,
strongly urges upon the Government the absolute
necessity for so rearranging the constituencies that
a fair system of proportional representation shall
be the basis of any new electoral law; and pledges
itself to support only such measures of political
reform as ensure a perfect system of equal franchise
for county and borough; equal voting power for
every elector; and a wider choice in the selection
of candidates as the only sound basis for securing
the direct representation of labour in Parliament
at the next general election.

Mr. Howell seconded the resolution.
Mr. Mottershead and Mr. Williams supported
the resolution, which was passed.
Mr. George Hemming proposed that the Con-
ference should be held annually, at different towns,
to be decided upon hereafter.
Mr. Williams seconded the motion, and it was
carried.

It was decided to have the next conference at
Manchester.
A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the
conference.

THE EVENING MEETING.

A meeting was held in the Town Hall in the
evening, at which Mr. R. Marsden Latham pre-
sided.

The Chairman, in commencing the proceedings,
said that that meeting was an evidence that they
were not going to fall in the work upon which
they had entered. The good sense of Birmingham
men in selecting the objects for which they con-
tended, and their courage and zeal in fighting for
them, inspired the belief that by that agitation for
labour representation they were going to add an-
other grand and decisive victory to those already
won by the masses or the people, in favour of
justice and right. Outside and beyond the many
questions of a political character upon which there
was not complete agreement among working men,
there were many working men's own special ques-
tions—questions having reference to his position
as a worker, to his condition at home among his
children, to his happiness, independence, and his

general well-being. To those questions working
men should attach more than ordinary importance,
and to promote them they should sink minor diffe-
rences, and bring to their aid every necessary
agency to make them thoroughly successful. To
secure victory, working men must put their trust
chiefly in themselves, because neither Whigs nor
Tories, as polit;cal parties, would take their ques-
tions up, nor would the classes above them look
with favour on s movement like the present, in
which they were so blind as to see nothing but
danger to their interests. Having pointed out
that under the present state of things the producers
of wealth did not receive a fair proportion of it to
reward them for their ceaseless toil, he said the
existing state of things presented a practical in-
justice which it.was their interest to put an end to.
Bld as matters were with workers in towns, they
were worse with the agricultural labourers. To
produce the necessary reforms working men must
be sent to Parliament—men who could help to
shape opinion, and who would insist on discussing
the most venerable and respectable abuses. They
wanted :non of stronger thought and more earnest
and direct speech than ever their best friends of
other classes could give them. Representatives of
their own order would know how far their intelli-
gence was insulted and their patience was tried by
the present state of things, and they would be
able to speak with authoritylas to the danger of
delay in the work of reform. The speakers who
would address them that evening would bring for-
ward a series of resolutions, which had been
adopted at a conferenee held in the afternoon, but
for which the confirmation of that meeting was
desired. (Applause.)
Mr. John Kane, of Darlington, secretary of the
National Association of Ironworkers, moved the
following resolution
That in the opinion of this meeting, considering
the probable early dissolution of Parliament, the
time has arrived for a determined effort to be made
to organise the working class by means of its
various associations, with a view to secure direct
representation of labour in the House of Com-
mons.

He said every effort should be made by working
men to get themselves thoroughly organised in
order to put an end to an anomaly which ought
not to exist in what were called reformed institu-
tions. Ile contended that men of their own order
could be found who would efficiently represent
them, and they ought to make it their business to
ace that they were represented by such. Let them
not be frightened by the cry of splitting the
Liberal interests. They had no interest but their
own. Their own interest should be all to them.
Divide the Liberal interest, indeed! What was
the Liberal interest ? That only should be to
them the Liberal interest which was calculated to
produce more social comfort for them. The Whig
party had discarded their old name and assumed
that of "Liberal." They were liberal
.with the
freedom and power of the working classes, but
they were not liberal in tendering to them their
fair share of power. If the working classes voted
honestly for their own order they were sure of
success. But even if they failed, it was better to
fight a losing battle for principle rather than a suc-
cessful one without it. (Applause.)
Councillor Airey, of Worcester, a working man,
seconded the resolution. He urged that it was not
fair that labour should be unrepresented in the
house of Commons. The Liberals bad alviays
been put into power by the working men, and he
believed the time was now come when the Liberal
leaders ought to help the working men to return
a few candidates of their own order.

REMINISCENCES Or TEE Prars-
SIAN POLICE.

The following anecdotes of the tyranny prac-
tised by the Prussian police are from an authentic
source, and may be relied upon as true:—
M. Henry, an old gentleman who lived for more
than twenty-five years in Prussia, fell ill, and his
Wife wrote to their son—who was established in
the United States of America—to come over and
see his old father once more before his end. The
dutiful son threw all his business aside, went on
board the first steamer bound to Hamburg ; where
he arrived in due time. By the first tram he set
off for Berlin. Here, he was stopped by the
pelice, who asked for his passport. 'Young Mr.
Henry, little versed in police matters, had not
even thought of a passport. When he left home
be had none. A republican u ithout a psssport,
What a horror! Of course he was arrested on the
spot as a vagabond, put into prison, and com-
pelled to spin wool. In this agreeable eituation
he remained for ten days; after which:time he be-
came free, by the interposition of the American
consul in Hamburg, to whom be wrote imme-
diately after his arrest. The Prussian police did
not even apologize to him. They simply told him,
" All right; you have told us the truth, and may
IVO The misused gentleman was almost killed
by this vexation, and took the product of his
labours in the spineing-house (a large clew ol
worsted) home with him, to show it to his
children, and to keep it in his family as a token
of Prussian liberty.
Another gentleman I know well remained in
prison a whole year for having irreverently ob-
served upon one occasion that the king was
tipsy,
1. was intimately acquainted with a literary man
who conducted a weekly newspaper; the cheap-
ness of which (three shillings a year) was thought
more dangerous even than its contents. It was
written under censure; that is to say, the proof.
sheets were sent to the censor, who struck out
everything which he considered disloyal. Having
thus received the sanction of the Government,
the paper was published, and common-sense
would have induced every editor to think himself
safe. It was not so. My friend had an immense
success with his paper, and got, in a few months,
no fewer than fifteen thousand subscribers. This
would have yielded him a considerable income,
even after 'English notions. All the German
Governments, and most of all that of Prussia, be-
came almost frantic; for my friend was as
cautious as clever, and they could not get at him
under any legal pretext. One day, however,
when I was at dinner wondering at my friend's
vacant place I received a hurried,, open pencil-
note from him, dated from prison; by which ho
informed me of his having been arrested, and of
the judge's having very reluctantly consented to
let him go, on depositing five hundred tbalers in
cash. Fortunately the money was to he had. I
took it myself to the judge, and delivered my
friend.
Of course I was curious to know his offence,
and was not a little amused whtn he showed me
the lines of his paper for which the Austrian Go-
vernment had impeached him. He had spoken of
an Austrian chief of artillery havieg oppOsed the
reducing of military service from fourteen years to
eight, objecting that it would be impossible for re-
cruits to become good artillerymen in eight years;
and the writer exclaimed, • that a fellow who
could not learn his service in eight years must be
indeed a potenzirter Austrian ;" which meant, that
he must be many times sillier than the Austrians
generally are thought to be in the north of Ger-
mans:. My friend was condemned to three months'
imprisonment without being alloWed to compound
for his punishment by a payment of money; which
was customary in press transgressions. Very soon
afterwards the paper was prohibited without any
legal proceeding—nay, against law and constitu-
tion.
When my friend published another journal, that
wag prohibited also, and we got a hint that he
would be arrested. By stratagem I got his pass-
port from the bureau where it was deposited, and
he left Leipzig, going to the next Prussian town;
for he was a subject of Prussia. Taught by
necessity, any friend was well versed in the law,
and adhered so strictly to it, that they could find
no "legal pretexts " fur a long time; but he was
annoyed in every manner. At last the Prussian
Government, who would put him aside at any cost
—sent one of his books to Magdeburg-, that the law
officers and judges there might pick out from
it matter to impeach him for high treason, or any
other nonsense that promised a rich harvest of
prison. The Magdeburg court were much puzzled
by this desire of the Government; for they could
find no crime in the book, and returned it at last
to Berlin. But very soon it came back, with a
reproof, and many passages in the book marked
with a red pencil. Cardinal Richelieu said, "Give
me five written words of a man, and I shall find
matter in them to have him 'hanged." My friend
was summoned before the court, and impeached on
Ilajestats-Beleidigung-ssleses majestatis is, I think,
the technical IMMO. When theiudges showed him
the offeeding passage he took the Landreobt (pro-
vincial law) smilingly up from the table, turned
up the paragraph relating to the offence attributed
to him, and read aloud, "Such a criminal shall
be dragged to the place of execution sitting upon
a cowskin and there crushed by a wheel, &as.
(geradert werden von unten auf). And all this
for the flesh-coloured tricots of Lola Montoz ! The
whole court of justice could not help laughing
outright; for the thing was too ludicrous.
In his paper my friend had mentioned how Lola
Mentes had horsewhipped an officer of the police,
and how she had been conderaned to half a year in
the house of correction, but had been pardoned by
the King, and concluded: " Well, I winader
whether 1 should have been pardoned also for
having committed such a crime? Possibly, but
not likely; for if, even in the scale of justice, a
pair of tiesh-eoloured tricots weighs heavier than
my steel pen, how much the more will they not
put out of its ersialiblriuni the balance of grace ?"

Yes; the judges
.Condetnned him, laughingly, to
two year's imprisonment, and the loss of tbe na-
tional cockade. About this hated sign of bondage
to an absolute Hohenzollernmy friend cared not a
pin: but its loss involved the lose of most of his
civil rights. Therefore he laid art appeal against
this verdict, and it was altered to only one year
of imprisonment, which he endured, in the citadel
of Magdeburg.
So much for the press. , Now r shall show how
the police work in the vineyard of the Lord.
There was, in Konigsberg, a dissenting congre-
gation of about eight thousand members, belonging
to a Protestant sect spread all over the empire.
Of course any legal pretexts to be met with were
available for annoying and vexing these dissent
ers ; but the police used the most dastardly and
base means to ruin them besides, They induced,
for instance, all persons employed in the police,
and even private persons, to give no work to any
tradesmen, to buy no goods of merchants belong-
ing to this persecuted sect—nay, keepers of public-,-
houses and tea or coffee gardens were forbidden to
sell anything to members of it, limier pain of the
withdrawal of their licenses. This was a serious'
thing for these innkeepers, and they requested the
Reverend Mr. Rupp, then minister of the Congre-
gation, to communicate thrso police measures to 1
his parishioners, lest they might bring innocent
Men to trouble and ruin.
One of the dissenters, having no fewer ther ten
children, happened to be employed in the police,
and lost his place for his religion.. To get another
existence this man competed to rent the house of
the shooters' company belonging to the city. and
therefore depending on the city authorities. When
the police became aware of his intention, they.
managed things with the corporation so, that he
was offered the house only if he would receive the
Lord's Supper out of the hands of the roost fanatical
parson of the State church. The poor man, having
no other hope of supporting his large family, was
weak enough to eornplj ; but he was afterwards
very much troubled in his mind ; wretched for life,
in feet.
A young respectable girl, having a very large.
connection as a seamstress, against whom no One
in Konigsberg could say a word, belonged to the
dissenters ; and, not being a native of Ktinigsbeig,
although of Prussia, was ordered to leave the city
in a fortnight. The girl, whose nimble fingers
supported an old mother, was not base enough to
disown her faith, and prepared vreepingly to leave
her friends and her snug, although humble posi-
tion. However, she was not only clover and good,
but pretty, and a young mattrr-joiner offered her
his hand. She accepted him at onoe. . There was
no time for simpering; a fortnight with three
Sundays being just sufficient to fulfill the requisites
of the law. The night before the day she was
ordered to leave her home, the Reverend Mr. Rupp:
performed the marriage-service, and they sit joys
ously at supper, laughing at the police; for now,
being the bride of a citizen of Kiinigsberg, she was
legally a denizen of that city. A loud knock was
heard at the door. Police entered, and one of them
said, "This assembly is dissolved I" This inter-
ruption was disagreeable, but so ludicrous that
everybody was amused. The bridegroom said.
"Well, good night, friends—sorry for the good
victuals, but they might dissolve as much as they
like; this society" (he took the hand of his bride)
I think, shall never he dissolved; neither by any
policeman nor by any other functionary, whether
in blue or in black." ,
With this dissolving of assemblies the police
annoyed the dissenters most. Some of them had
little meetings to take tea and read the (Airman
classics. Almost always they were disturbed by
policemen dissolving the assembly; sometimes
followed by soldiers with their muskets and bay-
onets. The next day each member of this circle
was summoned before the polioe and reproved.
Remonstrance was unless ; and, when they at last
asked the president of the police to give them a
definition of a prohibited assembly (for they had
no idea why the Government should prohibit every
tea party) be told them their meeting was not to
be taken for a tea party, but for an assembly ;'
bo
cause the different persons forming it were neither
friends nor neighbours nor relations, nor of the
same station in life. When the Reverend Mr.
Rupp once invited some poor people of his congre-
gation to a publics garden, to keep hodday there,
he was reproved by the police. He remonetrated,
and said these persona had been his pests. He
was answered rudely, that they were low people,
and no society for him. Mr. Rupp took . out his
Bible and read a passage in St.. Luke, in which
something was said about not inviting the rich,
who could give dinner's in return, but the poor and
needy. The magistrate looked confused, and Mr.'
Rupp eseaped, unlined.
Even children-gardens were forbid by the police,
andan assembly of babies, from three to five years.
old, was once 'dissolved. • The little ones did not
know the way home; for it was not yet time to .be-
fetched by the servants of their parents, and, when
the police asked them the names of their fathers,
they answered, "Papa." Then the little lambs
were seen walking with the wolves, quite confi-
dently, about the streets, inquiring where they did
belong to.
Such dissentees as belonged to official
tamiliea
were persecuted most. The Lieut.-Colonel von
L., who died in the year eipteea hundred and
forty-eight, left two orphan girls, without a penny.
However, the younger eist-r had the expectancy
of a place as canonesse in a foundation for spinsters
of noble birth, which bad been restored and richly
bestowed by the late grandfather of the young lady,
who was a very rich man. The elder of the two
sisters got, after much ado, a small pension from
the Government, by the interest of the minister of
Auerswald, who was connected with the family.
Angelina, the younger sister, while expecting her
canonesse-place, mod to get livelihood by giv•
.ing lessons in French, and writing books for yOung
people.: Heiien,bleased her breve siudeavouri;
she got a situation at :a, school, and Many private
lessons. She had, indeed, so ranch to do, that al-
most her only recreation was to visit the religious
Congregations of the dissenters, to hear Mr. Rupp.

• Thus she went on very well till the year eight-
een hundred and fifty-two; when it was ordered
by .Polizei-President Peteis that Miss von L.
should forbear giving any lesson,; secondly,. it,
was decreed that 'Miss Leo, the mistress of the'
school, should dismiss .‘1 iss A. von L. directly, end,
without any fuss (geraenschlos) ; thirdly, 'Alias,
von L. was to leave Kaniirsberg, and informed
that the interdict to give any lessons
,applied to
the whole Prussian rnonateby.
In vain the unhappy lady tried the law—ti y,
wrote even twiLe to the King, ooniplaining of t
he
wrongs practised on her. She was answered by
the Minister of the Interior, that all the proceed-
ings against her had been strictly lawful. Not-
withstanding, Miss von L. tried to give lessons in
Dantzig, where the first magistrate was a friend
of her family •, but this gentlethan, although wir•h •
inc her well; found himself obliged to repeat the
proceedings of Kiinigsberg. She left the Prussian
empire for Dresden, where she found pUplls ; but
there came a telegraphic dispatch from Berlin,'
and she was ordered 'by the police of Saxony to
' leave Dresden in-twenty.eight hours. To fill the
chalice of sorrow to the brim, she received a letter
from the abbess of the Barth-foundation telling

her to give tip all expectation of a winociesse.plitile'
if she adhered to the dissenters. Thus she 'lest
home, existence—oven the only hope left her for
old age—for her faith.

articles.text:
STANDING GIIDIRS.

• 1. The Congress shall consist only of delegates
representing bona fide Trades Societies, and
Trades Councils, and similar bodies, by whatever
halite they may, for the time being, be called.
2. Each delegate shall come provided with a
credential signed by the officers of the society or
council he represents, certifying to his appoint-
ment, each credential to be given up to the Secre-
tary, immediately on his arrival at the Con-
gress.

3. The time of meeting shall be as follows :
on the first • day to assemble at 12 o'clock noon
prompt; on all ether days at 0 30 a.m. ; adjourn
at 1, re-assemble at 2, and adjourn at 6 o'clock
each day.
4. The roll shall be called promptly to time
morning and afternoon, the names of all del°4
gates late er absent to be read over with the
minutes each morning.
6. At the opening-of the annual Congress, the
Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee shall
take the chair pro forma until the Congress has
elected its own President.
0. A connnittee of three shall be elected to
examine the credentials, and report thereon to the
meeting.

7. The deletes shall then proceed to elect the
President of the Congress, preference being given
to a delegate of the town where the Congress is
being held.

8. The Congress shall then elect a Secretary, It,
like preference being given.
9. The Congress shall then elect a vice-Presi-
dent, a deorikeeper and a messenger.
10. A standing committee. of five shall then be
elected, to whom shall be remitted the whole
business of the Congress; the order of and subjects
far discussion, together with the whole financial
arrangements of the Congress. The vice-president
to be the chairman of the committee. _

li, After thb routine business of election of
officers and committee, the pteeident shall formally
open the Congress with an address.
• 12. The standing committee, with a view to
securing a proper despatch of bueiness, with perfect
feitnets to all who have been to the trouble to
ptepare papers, cif which due notice has been
given, shall have pawed' to divide the Congress
into sections, so that those specidlly interested in
any particular question may have the Wept
opportunity for its discussion.
la. 'the standing committee shall be allowed to
retire at 4 o'clock each day (one hour *before•
closing the sittings of Congreas), for the purpose
of selecting and arranging the next day's pro-
gramme.
14. Each delegate shall pay to the treasurer, on
the first day of his arrival, the sum of Ns. towards
the expenses of the Congress ; and in ease he
represents more than one society, Ws. for every
such aociety he is delegated to represent. The
names of those *ho have, and those who have not
paid, to be read over when the roll im called on the
following inorning. No person steill be demand a
membet. of Congtess until his levy is paid.
18. TIM reader of a paper shall be allowed
twenty minutes; the meter of resolution fifteen
minutes; succeeding speakers ton minutes each;
no one shall speak more than once on any one
question. After the reply, no one shall be allowed
to spedk oft the question before the chair, but it
shall be at once put tO the vote by the chairman.
16. No second amendment, or rider to an ori-
ginal proposition, shall be put to the vote until
the first amendment is disposed of.
17. The voting shall be by show of hands; but
in ease of a dispute, the chairman may order a
division. _

18. Two tellers shall be appointed by the Con-
gress, and their ruling shall be fine'.
19- If more than one amendment is proposed,
the standing committee may retire, together with
the movers of the resolution and amendments, for
the purpose of trying to secure unanimity, by
blending the amendments in such a manner WI will
be most condueive to the harmony of Congress
and the despatch of business.
20. No delegate shall be allowed to read a
second paper until after all other papers' of which
notice has been previously given, have been read,
unless by special permission and sanction of the
standing committee, and the formal consent of
Congress.
21. In the selection of papers to be read, pre-
ference shall be given to those of which notice has
been given, and in the order in which they have
been received by the committee.
22. Subjects having special reference to the
trade of the town or locality where the Congress
is being held, shall in no ease be allowed to oc-
cupy the time of more than one sitting of the
congress. And it is desirable that these special
subjects be laid before the committee as early as
practicable, for the purpose of arranging them
under one or two general heads, and embodying
them in one or two simple propositions.
23. No delegate shall leave the room without
the consent of the Viee-Pkesident: and delegates
absent one whole sitting without leave of absence,
shall be named by the Chairman.
24. A. General or Parliamentary Committee of
nine shall be elected on the last clay of eitalz Con-

gross, who shall continue in office until they
are re-elected, or their successors are appointed.
They shall " elect from among themselves a
President, Treasurer, and Secretary for the
ensuing year; and they also shall remain in
office until they are re-elected, or their tinccesiors
are appointed.
25. All surplus monies, after payment of the
expenses of the Congress, shall be handed over to
the Treasurer of the Parliamentary Committee for
the general purposes of such Committee.
26. The duties of the Parliamentary Com-
mittee shall be (I) to watch all legislative
measures directly affecting the questions or labour,
and (2) to initiate, whenever necessary, such
legislative action as Congress may direct, or as the
exigencies of the time and circumst4aces may
demand.

27. The officers, under the direction of the
committee, shall have authority to solicit sub-
scriptions, donations, or ldvies, for the purpose of
defraying the expenses incurred by such corn-
Mittee ; -but the mode of payment shall be left
optional with each society as to whether it shal
pay by levy or donation.
28. The Congress having been formally opened
by the President, after the usual routine business
of electing officers and committee, the Parlia-
mentary Committee shall present their repo l t for
the past year, which shall be read by the Parlia-
mentary Secretary, and shall lay it on the table
for discussion by the Congress.
29. The Parliamentary Committee shall assist
and co-operate with the local committee of the
town where tho next Congress is to. be held, for
the purpose of making the arrangements as com-
plete as possible, and preparing the questions to
be disousied, and together to take such joint action
as the business or other special circumstances of
the time may render necessary or desirable.
30. The Parliamentary Committee, in conjunc-
tion with the local committee, shall be empowered
to invite persons to attend the sittings of the Con-
gress whose presence they may deem advisable
and deiirable such persons to be allowed to
address the dongreas on the invitation of thd
Chairman.
